records.title: AgentForge: Execution-Grounded Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Autonomous Software Engineering

evidence_notes.finding: A five-role pipeline (Planner, Coder, Tester, Debugger, Critic) with mandatory sandboxed execution of every patch resolves 40.0% of SWE-bench Lite tasks versus 14.0% for a same-model single-agent baseline and 12.0% for ReAct. Ablations attribute the gain jointly to execution feedback (Tester-Debugger loop) and role decomposition, at roughly 2.7x the per-task API cost.
evidence_notes.quote: AGENTFORGEachieves 40.0% task resolution, outperforming the single-agent baseline by +26.0% and the ReAct baseline by +28.0%.

extraction.framework: AgentForge
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench Lite (300 tasks; 100-task ablation subset)
extraction.baseline: single-agent GPT-4o, ReAct (GPT-4o), published SWE-agent
extraction.key_results: 40.0% resolve / 37.5% patch rate vs 14.0% / 12.5% single-agent and 12.0% / 11.0% ReAct. Ablation on 100 tasks: full 42%, w/o Critic 38%, w/o Debugger 31%, w/o Tester 28%, w/o Planner 19%, single-agent 14%. Retry gains saturate after N=2. Failure modes on 30 sampled failures: faulty localization 40.0%, ineffective patch generation 26.7%, cognitive deadlock (repeated identical failing attempts) 20.0%, environment/tooling 13.3%. Cost 13,600 input + 5,100 output tokens ($0.1445/task) vs $0.054 single-agent, about 2.7x.
extraction.limitations: Operates at file-level granularity and struggles with multi-file coordination; binary resolve metric does not capture partial correctness or regressions; results rely on a single base model (GPT-4o) with one sample per agent and a fixed retry budget; strict sandbox limits (512 MB, 0.5 CPU, 30 s, no network) bound achievable performance; Tester-generated tests are sometimes brittle, weakening the execution-feedback signal; deployment still requires human oversight, static analysis, and audit.

records.title: Beyond Individual Intelligence: Surveying Collaboration, Failure Attribution, and Self-Evolution in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_notes.finding: Role heterogeneity buys division of labour but raises interdependence, so specialized multi-agent systems become more sensitive to interface mismatches, cascading error propagation, and coordination overhead; the survey argues failure attribution is unsettled because the point where an anomaly becomes observable rarely coincides with its origin.
evidence_notes.quote: As role diversity increases, so does interdependence among agents, making the system more sensitive to interface mismatches, cascading errors, and coordination overhead.

extraction.framework: surveys 12+ frameworks incl. MetaGPT, AutoGen, AgentVerse, AutoAgents, CAMEL, Generative Agents, Puppeteer, MASFactory
extraction.agent_count: 2 to unlimited across surveyed frameworks
extraction.baseline: single LLM agent (conceptual contrast)
extraction.key_results: Organizes the field into a four-stage 'LIFE' progression (Lay capability foundation, Integrate via collaboration, Find faults via attribution, Evolve via self-improvement) and formalizes dependencies between adjacent stages. Reports a design shift from homogeneous to heterogeneous role configurations and from static to dynamic role allocation; homogeneous agent teams get trapped in repeated self-consistency loops while heterogeneous ones incur interface mismatch and coordination overhead. Explicit text-based communication dominates but scales poorly: repeated broadcasting of long textual states creates token overhead, increases latency, and amplifies inconsistency when agents interpret shared context differently. Failure attribution challenges identified: the attribution target is defined inconsistently across studies; anomaly propagation is strongly coupled so observable failure point differs from true origin; fine-grained (step/module/type) attribution remains unreliable under long-horizon multi-role dependencies; and synthetic failure datasets built from templates or rule-based injection lack realism.
extraction.limitations: Secondary study with no new experiments; comparability across attribution methods is limited because input granularity, annotation targets, and evaluation criteria differ between primary studies; many dynamic-role systems are heuristic and do not learn when specialization helps versus when extra agents add noise; the cross-stage closed-loop agenda is proposed rather than validated.

records.title: Rethinking software engineering for agentic ai systems

evidence_notes.finding: As LLM and agentic code generation becomes abundant, verification rather than authorship becomes the rate-limiting activity; AI-generated defects are syntactically plausible but semantically flawed, so they evade superficial review and require layered hybrid verification pipelines plus accountable human oversight.
evidence_notes.quote: Unlike traditional defects, these failures often evade superficial review due to their syntactic plausibility.

extraction.key_results: Multivocal review of 23 studies synthesized into four pillars and a competency framework: intent articulation, systematic verification, multi-agent orchestration, and accountable human judgment. Argues verification should be treated as infrastructure rather than a discrete phase, combining LLM reasoning with static analysis, dynamic testing, and formal methods, since LLMs act as both generators and verifiers and can share correlated failure modes. Cites a two-phase controlled experiment with 151 professional developers where AI assistance gave a 30.7% median reduction in task completion time in Phase 1 but no significant difference in completion time or code quality in Phase 2 when other developers evolved the code without AI, concluding maintainability depends on surrounding process infrastructure rather than the generative model. Notes an 'AI drag' effect where assistants boost senior engineers but impose a productivity drag on early-in-career developers, and that no single agent configuration is universally optimal so orchestration must be adaptive. Roadmap covers verification-first lifecycles, prompt provenance standards, auditability, liability attribution, and longitudinal workforce studies.
extraction.limitations: Construct validity is weak because 'agentic workflow' and 'orchestration' lack accepted definitions; external validity is bounded by a narrow time window and source set in a fast-moving field, with evidence drawn mainly from controlled or large industrial contexts; internal validity varies because multivocal sources differ in rigor and include non-validated perspectives; the proposed transformation framework is synthetic and conceptual, and its practical effectiveness awaits longitudinal real-world validation.

records.title: Llm-based agentic systems for software engineering: Challenges and opportunities

evidence_notes.finding: A concept-paper review across the SDLC argues multi-agent specialization improves modularity, tool use, and parallelism, but that current SE benchmarks measure isolated tasks and therefore cannot assess the cooperative capabilities that multi-agent systems are supposed to provide.
evidence_notes.quote: Existing benchmarks have focused on individual SE tasks and exhibit limitations as SE projects grow in complexity.

extraction.framework: reviews CrewAI, LangGraph, Google ADK, AutoGen, n8n; protocols CNP, A2A, ANP, MCP; systems incl. MARE, SpecGen, PairCoder, CodeAgent, GPTLens, LLIFT, CoverUp, WhiteFox, GPTDroid, AgentFL, ChatRepair, AutoSD
extraction.agent_count: 2 to 6 across reviewed systems (e.g. PairCoder 2, CodeAgent 6)
extraction.benchmark: discusses HumanEval, GSM8K, PURE, PROMISE, BugBench, Tests4Py
extraction.baseline: single LLM / standalone prompting (e.g. AUTOFL single-agent fault localization)
extraction.key_results: Systematic review of LLM-based multi-agent systems across five SDLC stages (requirements engineering, code generation, static code checking, testing, debugging). Claimed multi-agent advantages: per-task specialization, independent upgradeability/modularity, complementary perspectives, superior tool use, and parallel execution. Reports MARE surpassing SOTA text-parser and logical-reasoning baselines by 15.4% on requirements tasks. Identifies five forward challenges: agents can only simulate generic roles (developer, product manager) and lack SE-specific expertise such as vulnerability detection or security auditing; human-agent coordination (intervention points, feedback mechanisms) is underexplored; SDLC-wide data beyond code is needed; computational cost must be reduced via distillation, lightweight fine-tuning, and fewer inter-agent iterations; and cooperative-capability benchmarks are missing.
extraction.limitations: Concept paper with no new empirical evaluation; the review of selected works is described as concise rather than exhaustive; comparative evaluation of multi-agent design patterns (planner-executor pairs, self-refinement loops, human-in-the-loop) and empirical evaluation across open-source and proprietary LLMs are deferred to future work; deployment concerns around reliability, privacy, dynamic agent discovery, and cost management are raised but not measured.

records.title: The Rise of Agentic Testing: Multi-Agent Systems for Robust Software Quality Assurance

evidence_notes.finding: A three-agent closed loop (generation, execution/analysis, review/optimization) with sandboxed execution feedback raises statement coverage from 72.8% to 94.9% and valid executable tests from 64.1% to 89.3% over a single-pass LLM baseline, but the authors report non-deterministic LLM behavior, coordination latency, and context drift as persistent reliability threats.
evidence_notes.quote: Although agentic systems enhance adaptability, they remain subject to non-deterministic LLM behavior

extraction.framework: Agentic Testing Architecture (ATA); LangChain orchestration, Kubernetes, FAISS, RabbitMQ
extraction.benchmark: 8 open-source repositories plus 2 internal enterprise applications (~4,000 LoC per module), Python/Java/JavaScript/Node.js
extraction.baseline: single-pass static LLM (GPT-4o-mini) test generation without feedback loops
extraction.key_results: Mean statement coverage 72.8% -> 94.9% (+30.3%); branch coverage 61.5% -> 91.7% (+49.2%); valid executable tests 64.1% -> 89.3% (+39.3%); runtime per module 3.5 h -> 1.1 h (-68.6%); QA validation effort 11.8 -> 3.4 person-hours (-71.2%). Convergence typically at 4-6 iterations (Python) and 5-7 (Java), mean 5.2. Persistent cross-agent vector memory prevented reintroduction of prior failure contexts, a limitation the authors attribute to single-model setups. Abstract claims up to 60% reduction in invalid tests and 30% coverage improvement.
extraction.limitations: Non-deterministic LLM outputs undermine reproducibility, especially in regulated or safety-critical settings; computational footprint grows with agent count and feedback cycles, and cited work reports context synchronization degrading beyond four concurrent reasoning agents due to token overlap and memory contention; persistent shared memory introduces semantic/embedding drift requiring context pruning and rolling windows; human oversight is still needed to prevent overfitting and self-confirming bias loops; multi-agent reasoning chains obscure accountability, motivating embedded provenance metadata; bias in training data can cascade through the generation pipeline.

records.title: Iterative Audit Convergence in LLM-Managed Multi-Agent Systems: A Case Study in Prompt-Engineering Quality Assurance

evidence_notes.finding: Iterative full-scope LLM auditing of a seven-lane multi-agent prompt-specification surface surfaced 51 defects over nine non-monotonic rounds; cross-lane data-contract defects were undetectable by single-file review by construction and only appeared once multi-file context loading was enabled.
evidence_notes.quote: By construction, single-file review cannot detect cross-lane data-contract issues; in this study every cross-lane defect surfaced only after multi-file context loading was enabled.

extraction.framework: AEGIS (Autonomous Engineering Governance and Intelligence System)
extraction.agent_count: 7 lanes (seven-lane production pipeline), audited by an LLM sub-agent inspector
extraction.benchmark: none standard; 7152-line eight-document specification surface plus a released public synthetic mini-specification with 5 seeded defects
extraction.baseline: single-file review and one-pass audit (described conceptually; a single-pass full-scope control was NOT run)
extraction.key_results: 51 consistency defects surfaced across nine rounds (per-round 15, 8, 12, 2, 8, 1, 4, 1, 0), converging non-monotonically; Mann-Kendall trend significant (p = 0.008, tau = -0.72) but reported descriptively due to round non-independence. Seven-category post hoc defect taxonomy with coding rules. Cascading edits observed: fixing a defect in round 5 created a newly incorrect changelog reference caught in round 6. Cross-LLM partial replication with four frontier vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI; 12 traces) found vendor blind spots were non-overlapping and the multi-vendor union detected all five seeded defects. Inter-rater reliability on a stratified 18-defect subsample: Cohen's kappa = 0.80 on category, 0.46 on severity. Automated verification greps caught structural issues but missed semantic drift.
extraction.limitations: Single system (n = 1) with no control group; the same LLM family (Claude) both authored and audited the specifications, so a clean pass shows internal consistency rather than ground-truth correctness; the seven-category taxonomy is post hoc, single-coder, and possibly non-exhaustive; sample sizes are modest (9 rounds, 51 defects) and rounds are not independent draws because audit scope expanded during the study; with a stochastic auditor and no repeat trials, the round-3 and round-5 bumps cannot be distinguished from auditor variance; the audit protocol co-evolved with discovered defects, so later prompts may be tuned to the known defect space and fix ordering may have shaped category progression; convergence to zero findings establishes internal consistency, not correctness; no single-pass full-scope control, no human-only or hybrid review, and no multi-system replication; operational outcomes of the fixes are out of scope.

records.title: Understanding multi-agent LLM frameworks: A unified benchmark and experimental analysis

evidence_notes.finding: Under a fixed LLM and identical tasks, framework-level architectural choices alone drive over 100x latency differences, up to 30% planning accuracy loss, and coordination success collapsing from above 90% to below 30%, indicating multi-agent behavior is governed by execution semantics and interface design rather than model quality.
evidence_notes.quote: Our results show that framework-level design choices alone can increase latency by over 100×, reduce planning accuracy by up to 30%, and lower coordination success from above 90% to below 30%.

extraction.framework: MAFBench evaluating LangGraph, n8n, Langflow, CrewAI, AutoGen, OpenAI SDK, Agno, OpenAgents, DeepMind Concordia
extraction.agent_count: single-agent and multi-agent settings; coordination evaluated at scaling agent population sizes
extraction.benchmark: MAFBench (unified suite integrating existing benchmarks for orchestration, memory, planning, specialization, coordination)
extraction.baseline: direct LLM call (orchestration latency measured as multiplier of direct LLM) and single-agent settings
extraction.key_results: Orchestration latency 1.3x to 117x direct LLM; throughput 8.9 req/s down to <0.01. Overall memory score 23.8% (best) vs 6.1% (worst); memory forgetting fails universally because frameworks lack explicit memory editing and dependency-aware deletion. Planning accuracy change ranges +15% to -30% with 1.2x to 30x runtime multiplier; free-form natural-language planning generally helps while schema-constrained planning is a primary source of failure and overhead, converting correct reasoning into parsing/execution failures especially for local open models. Specialization delta F1 from about 0 to +58: professional role labels do not activate domain reasoning, but expert-guided procedural conditioning delivers large gains. Coordination task success at large n ranges >90% to <30% and is governed by communication topology, not interaction rounds, tokens, or model capacity; limited-hop neighbor-based topologies do best locally, sparse long-path graphs fail global agreement at scale, and only dense broadcast-style connectivity consistently enables system-wide consensus. Six design principles plus ORCA, a step toward automated multi-agent architecture selection.
extraction.limitations: The underlying LLM is fixed to isolate architectural effects (planning is the exception, evaluated across multiple LLMs), so results characterize framework architecture rather than model behavior; MAFBench integrates existing benchmarks under a standardized pipeline rather than proposing new tasks, and existing benchmarks vary in format, assumptions, and protocols requiring re-engineering; identified open gaps include lack of controlled forgetting, dependency-aware revision, contradiction resolution, memory growth guarantees, lifecycle management and versioning for procedural expertise, and runtime guarantees on convergence, stability, and cost as agent populations scale.

records.title: Observability and Fault Injection for LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems in Software Engineering

evidence_notes.finding: Trace-aligned fault injection shows perturbations at inter-agent communication boundaries propagate more damagingly than equivalent perturbations at single LLM calls: in ChatDev a 1000 ms A2A delay produced 59.2x mean runtime amplification versus 48.1x for an LLM delay, and 1.295x vs 1.053x in a minimal two-agent demo.
evidence_notes.quote: Overall, these results highlight that in a multi-phase, message-heavy workflow, the runtime impact of small injected delays can be magnified dramatically

extraction.framework: llmmas-otel (OpenTelemetry tracing + fault injection), validated on a Planner->Coder demo and on ChatDev
extraction.agent_count: 2 (demo Planner/Coder); ChatDev multi-agent across design, coding, testing phases
extraction.benchmark: ProgramDev (30 tasks), 5 runs per task per condition
extraction.baseline: fault-free baseline run of the same workflow, structurally aligned with faulty runs
extraction.key_results: Defines a trace model spanning session, segment (workflow phase), agent step, A2A send/receive, tool call, and LLM call spans with a stable attribute vocabulary. Supports faults at three boundaries: A2A send (delay, drop, truncate), A2A receive (delay, drop), tool call (delay, not_installed, timeout, malformed_response), and LLM call (delay, rate_limit, timeout, network_error, malformed_response). Amplification (extra end-to-end runtime / injected delay): demo LLM delay mean 1.053 (median 1.036), demo A2A delay mean 1.295 (median 1.390); ChatDev LLM delay mean 48.1 (median 13.9), ChatDev A2A delay mean 59.2 (median 6.6). Fault injection is an overlay on the same span structure so baseline and faulty runs stay comparable.
extraction.limitations: Initial validation only, on one minimal demo workflow and one real system (ChatDev); fault injection currently covers just three runtime boundaries (A2A, LLM, tool) and does not yet include higher-level workflow, memory-related, or coordination faults; the tool provides no higher-level analysis such as paired-run differencing, trace summarization, root-cause ranking, or automated debugging reports, so users must inspect traces manually; large gap between demo and ChatDev median vs mean amplification indicates high run-to-run variance.

records.title: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Automated Software Testing

evidence_notes.finding: A four-agent testing framework reaches 55.0% differential defect detection on QuixBugs versus 37.5% for a same-model single-agent baseline, and the ablation attributes that 17.5-point advantage to role decomposition rather than to the dedicated diagnostic agent; the conventional unconditional criterion overstates detection by 35 points (90.0% vs 55.0%).
evidence_notes.quote: Role decomposition is supported: the single-agent condition, run with the same model and the same budget, detects 17.5 fewer points under the differential criterion.

extraction.framework: four-agent multi-agent testing framework (requirement analysis, test-case generation, sandboxed execution, defect detection) on GLM-4-Flash
extraction.benchmark: QuixBugs (40 Python programs, 14 defect classes)
extraction.baseline: same-model single-agent configuration of the same framework; also diagnosis-only and execution-only ablations
extraction.key_results: Differential detection (two-run protocol against reference implementation, recommended primary indicator) 55.0% (SD 3.1) vs 90.0% unconditional and 5.0% strict; the 35-point gap is traced to LLM test artifacts, mainly hallucinated oracle values and signature mismatches. Same-model single-agent baseline reaches 37.5% differentially (-17.5 points). Removing the diagnostic agent costs only 2.5 points differentially, within seed-to-seed variation, and diagnosis-only is the worst of four conditions; the composite rule's extra detections do not survive the differential check. Failure analysis: 9 of 18 differentially undetected programs get suites that execute and fail but fail identically on correct code (oracle quality), with input construction and path coverage accounting for the other 9. Cost about 9,300 tokens and 143 s per program.
extraction.limitations: Single benchmark (QuixBugs: 40 moderate-size single-line-fault programs), limiting generalization to industrial code with module interplay, race conditions, and specification-implementation mismatch; every detection occurred in the first round across all five runs so the iterative feedback loop is an architectural capability with no demonstrated empirical effectiveness on this benchmark; all conditions use one model (GLM-4-Flash) so framework effects cannot be separated from model effects; test quality assessed only via execution outcomes with no human evaluation of readability or maintainability; attribution categories in the failure table are lower bounds and the attributable count of nineteen is an upper bound; the only controlled comparison is against a single-agent configuration of the same framework, not against other architectures; the differential protocol requires a reference implementation that a live repository lacks; per-unit cost figures are a lower bound.

records.title: Automated Black-Box Testing: A Comparative Study of LLM Agent Architectures and Prompt Engineering

evidence_notes.finding: On HumanEval black-box unit-test generation, prompt engineering rather than architecture is the primary driver: multi-agent collaborative and competitive configurations achieve marginally higher coverage (peak 99.54%) but statistically comparable execution success to a single agent (96.98% vs 96.89%) while consuming 3-4x the tokens.
evidence_notes.quote: Although multi-agent architectures achieve superior test coverage — peaking at 99.54% — they yield an ESR comparable to single-agent frameworks (96.98% versus 96.89%).

extraction.framework: extended QA Agent framework (Deo et al.) with collaborative Merge/Concat and Competitive LLM-scorer patterns; base model nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b
extraction.agent_count: multiple (single-agent baseline vs multi-agent collaborative and competitive configurations, incl. a Code Architect role)
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval (full 164 problems and a curated 20-problem harder subset), 10 independent runs
extraction.baseline: single-agent LLM configuration under the same prompting strategy; also GPT-4 Turbo QA Agent and AgentCoder reference results
extraction.key_results: Rule-augmented few-shot prompting improves coverage and Execution Success Rate by 20-30% over zero-shot across all architectures. Single-agent with rule-augmented few-shot: ESR 96.98%, coverage 99.30% on the full dataset, at minimum token cost, versus ESR 62.17% / coverage 68.23% zero-shot. Best multi-agent (Merge Concat, rule-augmented few-shot): ESR 96.41%, coverage 99.54%. Multi-agent gains are largest under plain few-shot (ESR up to +5.56% curated, +2.91% full; coverage up to +2.19% curated, +3.21% full) and shrink under rule-augmented prompting. On the harder curated subset multi-agent always beat single-agent; on the easier full dataset a single agent matched or exceeded it. Multi-agent costs roughly 3-4x the single-agent token volume, a non-proportional increase for marginal accuracy gains.
extraction.limitations: Only a single benchmark dataset (HumanEval) is used, which the authors state is the main threat to external validity; curated-subset results are unexpectedly higher than full-dataset results, possibly because of affinity between selected tasks and the few-shot examples; the isolated effect of adding rules without few-shot examples was not measured; performance variation across task difficulty was not analyzed in depth; the reference-work comparison uses a different (stronger) base model; no critic agent or iterative feedback loop is included in the tested architectures.

records.title: A Comparative Empirical Evaluation of Single-Agent and Multi-Agent LLM Prompting Strategies for Automated Formative Feedback in Education

evidence_notes.finding: A tri-role multi-agent pipeline (Evaluator, Student Simulator, Reviewer) produced the highest composite quality (CQS 4.21/5) and lowest over-praise and hallucination rates, but consumed roughly 4.6x the tokens of a zero-shot single agent, while a chain-of-thought single agent reached 86.5% of the top score at 32.5% of its token cost.
evidence_notes.quote: The S4 strategy consumed approximately 4.6 times the tokens of S1, translating to proportionally higher API costs.

extraction.framework: four prompting configurations (S1 zero-shot single-agent, S2 chain-of-thought single-agent, S3 dual-role draft+critique, S4 tri-role Evaluator/Student Simulator/Reviewer) on GPT-4-Turbo
extraction.agent_count: 1 to 3
extraction.benchmark: 200 undergraduate argumentative essays; multi-dimensional rubric (accuracy, specificity, actionability, constructive tone, completeness) scored by 3 trained raters plus automated similarity to expert reference feedback
extraction.baseline: zero-shot single-agent (S1) and chain-of-thought single-agent (S2)
extraction.key_results: Multi-agent configurations outperformed single-agent across all five rubric dimensions; S4 achieved the highest composite quality score (CQS = 4.21 on a 5-point scale) and the lowest rates across all four error categories (over-praise, over-inference, hallucination, omission). The multi-agent advantage is not uniform: stratified by instructor pre-score quartile, the S4-over-S2 CQS gap was 0.74 points for second-quartile essays but narrowed to 0.38 for top-quartile essays, indicating the largest incremental value where diagnostic complexity is highest. Mean tokens per feedback instance: S1 847, S2 1,264, S3 2,531, S4 3,892 (S4 about 4.6x S1). S2 delivers 86.5% of S4's CQS at 32.5% of its token cost, and S3 is proposed as a cost/quality compromise.
extraction.limitations: Single LLM (GPT-4-Turbo), so generalization to Claude, Gemini, or open-source families requires cross-model replication; the essay corpus comes from a single institution and a single discipline (English academic writing), limiting ecological breadth; only three human raters were used; feedback quality was evaluated as a static property of one interaction with no longitudinal measurement of student revision gains; no cross-disciplinary replication and no student perception or think-aloud data.

records.title: A Modular Multi-Agent {LLM} Architecture for Text-to-Diagram Generation and User-Guided Refinement

evidence_notes.finding: A deterministic validation agent wrapped in a bounded generate-validate-regenerate loop acts as a robustness amplifier that homogenizes output quality across ten heterogeneous LLM backends, so models differ mainly in first-attempt stability and latency rather than in ultimate ability to satisfy the specification.
evidence_notes.quote: Even for models with imperfect first-attempt behavior, the combination of deterministic validation and bounded regeneration significantly increases the final success rate.

extraction.framework: modular multi-agent text-to-diagram pipeline (Agent 3 meta-selector, Agent 5 synthesizer, Agent 7 deterministic validator, Agent 9 user-guided refiner)
extraction.benchmark: 30 prompts (20 easy, 10 complex) x 10 LLMs = 300 runs; metrics are final validation success, first-attempt success, validation iterations, error profile, latency
extraction.baseline: monolithic / single-pass single-model text-to-diagram generation (conceptual comparison)
extraction.key_results: On easy prompts most models reach 95-100% final success with high first-attempt rates; on complex prompts several models reach 100% final success but 0% first-attempt (kimi-k2-thinking, gpt-5-codex, grok-code-fast-1), while glm-4.6 and grok-4-fast reach 0% final success. Agent 7 error profiling separates syntax_errors, missing_nodes/missing_edges, invalid_attributes, style_violations, and other; non-successful runs are dominated by syntax errors with structural errors nearly absent, indicating that once syntax is correct the structural semantics usually match the specification. Style/flavor violations are rare, so stylistic guidance integrates without destabilizing structural correctness. Latency varies significantly across providers, creating a speed-versus-stability trade-off for interactive tools.
extraction.limitations: Only ten runs per model on the complex prompt set, which the author says should be interpreted with caution; benchmarks are largely flowchart- and ER-style diagrams, so broader complex specifications remain untested; no formal statistical testing or threats-to-validity section; semantic grounding via DSLs and graph-transformation backends, multimodal inputs, provenance, safety, and usability studies are all deferred to future work.

records.title: Designing LLM-based multi-agent systems for software engineering tasks: Quality attributes, design patterns and rationale

evidence_notes.finding: Across 94 papers on LLM-based multi-agent systems for SE, Role-Based Cooperation is the dominant design pattern (44 systems, 47.4%) among 16 identified patterns, chosen mainly to improve functional correctness and modularity, while performance efficiency (51.1%) and maintainability (50.0%) are traded off against each other.
evidence_notes.quote: Role-Based Cooperation is the design pattern most frequently employed among 16 patterns used to construct LLM-based MASs

extraction.framework: 94 LLM-based MASs incl. MetaGPT, MARE, MAAD, AgileCoder, AgentFL, FixAgent, CODER, INTERVENOR
extraction.agent_count: varies across the 94 surveyed systems (e.g. MAAD 4 role-dedicated agents, AgentFL 4 roles, planner/developer/reviewer triads)
extraction.benchmark: discusses DevBench and notes absence of a lifecycle-wide benchmark
extraction.key_results: Ten SE tasks identified with Code Generation most common; Functional Suitability is the most-considered quality attribute, with Functional Correctness explicitly targeted by 91.5% of systems; 16 design patterns identified with Role-Based Cooperation used by 44 (47.4%); the most common design rationale is Improving the Quality of Generated Code (44.7%), followed by Simulating Human Processes of Solving SE Tasks (29.8%), Optimizing Software Resource Management (28.7%), and Improving the Efficiency of Software Artifact Generation (24.5%). Performance Efficiency is considered by 51.1% and Maintainability by 50.0%, with 22.3% considering both; Modularity is the most frequent Maintainability sub-QA and is chiefly pursued via Role-Based Cooperation. End-to-End Software Maintenance (8.4%) and End-to-End Software Development (7.4%) remain rare, attributed to missing lifecycle-wide evaluation criteria, missing standard benchmarks for most development stages, and difficulty keeping artifact formats and semantics consistent across stages. Cites an empirical finding that one-pass and multi-pass prompting show no apparent output-quality difference while one-pass consumes fewer API calls.
extraction.limitations: Construct validity is threatened because data collection and extraction were manual and subject to individual bias, mitigated only by a pilot extraction; internal validity is not discussed since the study involves no experimental manipulation and supports no causal inference; findings describe what designers report rather than measured system outcomes, so pattern prevalence is not evidence of pattern effectiveness; open challenges noted include mismatches between user expectations and agent capabilities, ambiguities in communication protocols, and limited methods for validating results and quality of inter-agent interactions.

records.title: Comparing Single-Agent and Multi-Agent Strategies in LLM-Based Title-Abstract Screening

evidence_notes.finding: Across five coordination strategies and four 7-8B open-source models, a single-agent baseline with the best-matched model in few-shot mode outperformed every multi-agent alternative (recall 100%, precision 70.4%, F1 82.6%, WSS@95 43.4%), indicating model selection outweighs coordination strategy at this parameter scale.
evidence_notes.quote: Multi-agent strategies introduced coordination overhead without measurable benefit under the conditions of this study.

extraction.framework: PaSSER-SR platform with five strategies: S1 single-agent, S2 majority voting, S3 recall-focused OR ensemble, S4 confidence-weighted aggregation, S5 two-stage screening with debate; blockchain-verified audit trail (private Antelope chain, OpenTimestamps, Zenodo)
extraction.agent_count: 1 to 3 (single agent; 3-model ensembles; gate model plus 2-model debate panel)
extraction.benchmark: Gold Standard of 200 papers (190 for evaluation) from a 2,036-record corpus on blockchain-based e-voting; 25 GS configurations plus 5 full-corpus configurations
extraction.baseline: single-agent (S1) screening with each of Mistral 7B, LLaMA 3.1 8B, Granite 3.3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B in zero-shot and few-shot modes

evidence_notes.finding: A multi-vocal review of 114 academic and grey-literature sources finds that reliability, security, cost and verification problems in LLM multi-agent code generation are systemic architectural weaknesses rather than isolated model failures, and that current benchmarks provide insufficient evaluation of multi-agent collaboration and coordination. records.title: SPEAR: An Engineering Case Study of Multi-Agent Coordination for Smart Contract Auditing

evidence_notes.finding: In smart-contract auditing, a decentralized multi-agent design outperformed a centralized scheduler that implemented identical risk-aware planning and repair logic (F1 0.87 vs 0.83), with the advantage concentrated under injected failures rather than under normal conditions, at a measured coordination overhead of 4.2%.
evidence_notes.quote: SPEAR achieves higher overall effectiveness than all baselines, including a centralized scheduler that implements identical planning and repair logic.

extraction.agent_count: 5 specialized agents (Planning, Execution, Repair, Safe Actuation, Coordination)
extraction.benchmark: Damn Vulnerable DeFi (15 challenges, 10 runs per configuration); 500 security objectives from GitHub Solidity contracts; one DeFi protocol (47 contracts, 12 vulnerabilities)
extraction.baseline: Centralized Scheduler with identical planning/repair logic; Sequential Pipeline (Slither -> Mythril -> Echidna); Slither only; Slither + Mythril; plus ablations (No Protocols, No Autonomy, No Self-Healing, Rigid Pipeline)
extraction.key_results: SPEAR F1 0.87 (P 0.89 / R 0.85) vs Centralized Scheduler 0.83, Sequential Pipeline 0.82, Slither+Mythril 0.78, Slither only 0.73. records.title: From llms to llm-based agents for software engineering: A survey of current, challenges and future

evidence_notes.finding: Surveying 139 papers across six SE topics, the authors argue LLM-based agents extend single LLMs through role specialization, iterative refinement and tool integration, but that multi-agent workflow complexity introduces synchronization, state-consistency and cascading-misunderstanding problems that single LLM pipelines do not exhibit, with no unified agent definition or evaluation protocol available.
evidence_notes.quote: Traditional LLMs excel at isolated tasks but face limitations due to constrained context awareness, insufficient feedback mechanisms, and minimal autonomy.

extraction.benchmark: HumanEval, MBPP, HumanEval-ET, MBPP-ET, HumanEval-X, CodeSearchNet, Spider, BIRD, ToolBench, APIBench, CAASD
extraction.baseline: LLMs (single-model prompting/fine-tuning) compared against LLM-based agents across six SE topics
extraction.key_results: 139 papers reviewed across requirement engineering, code generation, autonomous decision-making, software design, test generation, and maintenance. Single-model approaches can reach high pass@k on established benchmarks, but agent-based systems show broader coverage of large-scale, multi-file tasks. Six named challenges: (1) no standardized agent definition or evaluation protocol; (2) workflow complexity and error propagation in multi-agent systems, where asynchronous interaction is more prone to cascading misunderstandings and state/semantic alignment remains open; (3) fragile tool integration; (4) weak cross-task generalization; (5) scarcity of interactive multi-turn simulation datasets; (6) cognitive transparency and trust. Agent-specific metrics (Win Rate, Agreement Rate, Execution Effectiveness, Cost Efficiency) supplement Pass@k.
extraction.limitations: Narrative survey without a formal systematic-review protocol or quality appraisal; the boundary between an LLM and an LLM-based agent is acknowledged to be unsettled, so classification of the reviewed work is partly judgmental; performance comparisons are drawn from heterogeneous primary studies rather than controlled experiments; benchmark coverage is skewed toward static input-output tasks that the authors say cannot evaluate negotiation, role conflict resolution, or tool-driven reasoning.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 12 Designer:Programmer agent pairs from 7 open-source LLMs on a single C programming task, convergence, role alignment and compilation success were not correlated: only DeepSeek-R1:DeepSeek-R1 converged and sustained a correct solution, several pairs achieved 100% compilation while never reaching a correct solution, and pairs that diverged after 3, 21 or 69 iterations never recovered.
evidence_notes.quote: This suggests that once a correct solution emerges, it tends to be preserved for a bounded number of iterations (≤ 69 in our study), while later recovery is unlikely.

extraction.framework: Lightweight custom Python controller enforcing deterministic turn-taking between a Designer agent and a Programmer agent (models served via Ollama 0.12.10)
extraction.key_results: 12 Designer:Programmer pairs from Gemma 2, Gemma 3, LLaMA 3.2, LLaMA 3.3, DeepSeek-R1, MiniCPM and Qwen3; temperature 0.5, max 4096 tokens, iteration cap 10,000, each pair run twice. Three success/failure patterns identified: SFP1 successful convergence, SFP2 non-initiating, SFP3 divergence. Only DeepSeek-R1:DeepSeek-R1 converged from the first iteration and sustained it, yet had only 3.29% compilation success and 68-95% 'No Code Found' turns. LLaMA3.2:LLaMA3.2 and Qwen3:Qwen3 reached 100% compilation success with strong role alignment but never started from the correct solution (Qwen3 37% semantic echoing). DeepSeek-R1:MiniCPM and LLaMA3.3:LLaMA3.3 dropped to 30-40% success with up to 62% failures. Divergent pairs (Qwen3:DeepSeek-R1, DeepSeek-R1:LLaMA3.3, LLaMA3.3:LLaMA3.3) had produced the correct solution in iteration 1 and diverged after 3, 21 and 69 iterations respectively, with no observed recovery. records.title: A comprehensive survey on benchmarks and solutions in software engineering of llm-empowered agentic system

evidence_notes.finding: Connecting 50+ benchmarks to prompt-based, fine-tuning-based and agent-based solution paradigms across 150+ papers, the survey argues that existing multi-agent SE frameworks rely on simplistic coordination (sequential pipelines or centralized orchestration) that cannot express real development workflows, and that no benchmarks measure coordination efficiency or communication overhead.
evidence_notes.quote: Current multi-agent frameworks often rely on simple coordination mechanisms such as sequential pipelines or centralized orchestration, which fail to capture the dynamic, iterative, and often non-linear nature of real software development workflows.

extraction.benchmark: 50+ benchmarks catalogued and mapped to solution strategies, spanning code generation, translation and repair (e.g. SWE-bench, HumanEval)
extraction.baseline: Taxonomic comparison of prompt-based vs fine-tuning-based vs agent-based paradigms
extraction.key_results: 150+ papers reviewed. Multi-agent role decomposition is the dominant agentic pattern, exemplified by MAGIS (Manager/Developer/QA Engineer), AgileCoder (Product Manager/Tester), MASAI (Test Template Generator, Issue Reproducer, Edit Localizer, Fixer, Ranker), Co-PatcheR (localization/generation/validation), XpandA (Explorer agents) and staged planners (Codes, LLMDFA, DRCodePilot, MarsCode). Identified coordination challenges: communication protocols between differently specialized agents, redundant or conflicting edits to the same codebase, dependency and precedence management, and resource allocation across the collective. Proposed directions include decentralized coordination protocols, shared memory architectures with consistent codebase views, conflict-resolution and distributed-consensus algorithms, temporal-logic verification of coordination protocols, complementary role pairing (creative generator with rigorous verifier; bottom-up implementer with top-down architect), plus new benchmarks measuring coordination efficiency and communication overhead. Also flags an accountability vacuum around IP attribution, liability, unsustainable compute scaling, developer deskilling, and the need for verifiable audit trails and provenance tracking.
extraction.limitations: Descriptive taxonomy without controlled experiments or quantitative meta-analysis; benchmark-to-solution mappings are derived from primary-study self-reports rather than re-execution; the survey explicitly notes that agents degrade on domain-specific languages, legacy codebases and specialized domains because training data is imbalanced, and that current evaluation does not measure coordination efficiency, communication overhead or graceful handling of dynamic requirements.

records.title: Traceability and Accountability in Role-Specialized Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines

evidence_notes.finding: Across 8 pipeline configurations of 3 frontier LLMs on 3 benchmarks, an unstructured Planner-Executor-Critic pipeline fell below a competent monolithic model, while adding a structured accountable handoff raised accuracy by up to 36.22 points; blame attribution showed the Planner dominates failure (error rate 7.35% for the best model vs 40.49% for the worst) at a cost of 2-3x spend and 8-10x latency.
evidence_notes.quote: Without clear roles and checks, errors compound across stages and accuracy falls below a competent single model.

extraction.framework: Traceable/accountable sequential pipeline with blame attribution (Planner -> Executor -> Critic), instrumented for stagewise repair/harm/no-op flags and error-origin assignment
extraction.benchmark: PythonIO (127 prompts), LogiQA (283 prompts), AGIEval (263 prompts)
extraction.baseline: Monolithic single-model end-to-end answering, plus Simple (non-accountable) pipelines of the same configurations
extraction.key_results: 8 ordered triples of GPT-4o (A), Claude Sonnet 4 (B) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (C). Accountable vs Simple pipeline accuracy deltas: PythonIO BBB +36.22 (61.42% -> 97.64%), BAB +33.07, CBA +27.56, CCA +26.78; AgiEval AAA +19.78 (57.41% -> 77.19%), ABC +9.50; LogiQA gains modest (CCA +3.76 to +6.99). A few configurations regressed slightly (AgiEval BAB -2.28, BCC -0.76; PythonIO BCC -0.78). Planner error rates: Gemini 7.35% (AgiEval) / 0.79% (PythonIO) / 15.19% (LogiQA); Claude 13.43/3.94/22.03; GPT-4o 40.49/11.02/28.62. Role behaviours: Claude best Executor (repair 10.01%, harm 0.25%); GPT-4o highest Critic repair (5.20%) but highest Executor harm (1.33%); Claude highest Critic harm (1.90%); Gemini lowest harm (0.25%) in both roles. Recommended casting: Gemini Planner -> Claude Executor -> GPT-4o Critic. Heterogeneous pipelines (CBA, CCA) frequently sit on the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier. Accountability cost ~2-3x spend and median latency from ~2s to 20-25s (roughly 8-10x slower).
extraction.limitations: Construct validity: all three benchmarks are multiple-choice, which makes blame attribution tractable but may not reflect open-ended real-world software engineering. Internal validity: blame assignment presumes ground-truth labels that are unavailable at runtime, so deployments would need proxies such as self-consistency checks, verifier agents or unit tests. External validity: results come from three proprietary LLMs inside a fixed evaluation window and may shift with model updates; extension to open-source models is left to future work.

records.title: A Survey for LLM Agent Trajectory Analysis: From Failure Attribution to Enhancement

evidence_notes.finding: Surveying 55 papers on LLM agent trajectory analysis, the authors show automated failure attribution remains weak: step-level attribution accuracy on the Who&When benchmark spans only about 25-52%, with agent-level accuracy substantially higher, and benchmark diversity is the field's bottleneck. Multi-agent failure taxonomies (MAST) attribute failures to specification issues, inter-agent misalignment and task verification.
evidence_notes.quote: In terms of reported accuracy, on the Who&When benchmark, reported step-level attribution accuracy varies substantially across techniques, ranging from about 25% [11] to 52% [39].

extraction.benchmark: Who&When (primary), TRAIL, AgentErrorBench, TraceElephant, AgentEval
extraction.baseline: Comparison of attribution paradigms (LLM prompting, causal inference, fine-tuned tracer models, dynamic intervention) against each other on Who&When
extraction.key_results: 55 papers (early 2025 to April 2026) organized along failure taxonomy, failure attribution, system enhancement, monitoring tools, and datasets/benchmarks. Four taxonomic perspectives, four attribution paradigms, three enhancement families. MAST identifies 14 failure modes in 3 categories: specification issues, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification (including premature termination). Most prevalent failure families across taxonomies: instruction and format fidelity; task planning and decomposition; interaction, state and coordination (step repetition and reasoning-action mismatch prevalent in multi-agent settings); knowledge and reasoning limits. Step-level attribution accuracy on Who&When ranges ~25% to 52%; TraceElephant currently ~33%. Agent-level accuracy is consistently higher than step-level; algorithm-generated systems are easier to attribute than hand-crafted ones; fine-tuning-based methods perform relatively best. Benchmarks are shifting toward full observability and unrecoverable-failure annotation.
extraction.limitations: The survey states comparability across attribution studies remains limited due to differences in datasets, observability settings and evaluation protocols; Who&When is almost the only benchmark built specifically for failure attribution, so benchmark diversity is a bottleneck; reported step-level accuracy is acknowledged as still limited; agent-level or step-level accuracy may not reflect real diagnostic utility.

evidence_notes.finding: With three agent architectures implemented on a unified toolset to remove engineering confounds, a Dev-Test multi-agent workflow beat a single agent (49.48% vs 45.72% requirement implementation rate) while a Design-Dev-Test workflow collapsed to 27.71%, showing multi-agent decomposition helps only when well structured; 55.8% of all failures originated in planning (requirement omission 27.9%, misinterpretation 22.2%) rather than code implementation.
evidence_notes.quote: The results in Table 5, clearly indicate that “Task Planning” is the primary bottleneck in current agent systems, accounting for 55.8% of all issues.

extraction.baseline: SDAgent-Single (single-agent workflow) on the identical toolset
extraction.key_results: Requirement implementation rate: SDAgent-DT 49.48% > SDAgent-Single 45.72% > SDAgent-DDT 27.71% (state-of-the-art agents fulfil roughly 50% of requirements). evidence_notes.finding: Testing 27 permutations of three local LLMs across three agent roles in the PathFinder GUI-testing multi-agent system, the hypothesis that heterogeneous specialist LLMs beat a single shared LLM was rejected per-site (homogeneous constellations won on specific websites) and only weakly supported across sites (best mixed 0.703 F1 vs 0.660 for all-Gemma2), a marginal difference.
evidence_notes.quote: We cannot accept our hypothesis H1, as one-model MALLMs tend to perform better on specifc websites.

extraction.framework: PathFinder (Multi-Agent LLM / MALLM framework for exploratory web GUI testing)
extraction.agent_count: 4 (Perceptron/summarization, System 1/decision-making, Entry Bot/data extraction, Oracle/validation); LLM varied across the first 3
extraction.baseline: Homogeneous (single-LLM-across-all-agents) MALLM constellations
extraction.key_results: 27 permutations of Mistral-Nemo, Gemma2 and Llama3.1 across 3 agent roles, on 4 e-commerce sites (demo1, demo2, ikea, netonnet), locally hosted via Ollama. H1 (mixed models beat a single model for a specific system under test) rejected; H2 (mixed models beat a single model for a generic system under test) accepted. Best cross-site F1: llama3.1/mistral-nemo/mistral-nemo 0.703 and mistral-nemo/mistral-nemo/gemma2 0.702, vs all-Gemma2 0.660 and all-Llama3.1 0.654; worst was mistral-nemo/gemma2/gemma2 at 0.306. Technical threats include web scraping/parsing failures on dynamic content and JavaScript, possible Ollama model-switching and API failures disrupting agent coordination, and workflow bugs that are hard to trace given system complexity. records.title: Hallucination to Consensus: Multi-Agent LLMs for End-to-End JUnit Test Generation

evidence_notes.finding: CANDOR decomposes JUnit test generation across specialized agents (Initializer, Planner, Tester, Inspector, Requirement Engineer, Panelist, Interpreter, Curator) and shows that a panel-discussion consensus over multiple reasoning LLMs is what suppresses oracle hallucination: ablating the panel costs 0.067-0.086 oracle correctness, and consensus-by-reasoning beats plain majority voting.
evidence_notes.quote: However, we found that these single-LLM approaches fall short on complex tasks, such as unit test generation.

extraction.framework: CANDOR (prompt-engineering-based multi-agent JUnit test generation; LLaMA 3.1 70B as basic LLM, DeepSeek R1 as reasoning LLM)
extraction.agent_count: 8 agent roles (Initializer, Planner, Tester, Inspector, Requirement Engineer, Panelist, Interpreter, Curator), with 3 parallel Panelist+Interpreter pipelines
extraction.benchmark: HumanEvalJava and a newly constructed LeetCodeJava (Medium and Hard splits); mutation analysis via PiTest
extraction.baseline: EvoSuite (search-based), LLM-Empirical (single-LLM prompt engineering), TOGLL (fine-tuned oracle generator), plus ablations w/o Planner, w/o Requirement Engineer, w/o Panel, and w/ majority Voting
extraction.key_results: Test prefixes: CANDOR line coverage 0.991/0.990/0.989 and branch 0.950/0.949/0.980 across the three datasets, statistically indistinguishable from EvoSuite (p>0.05) but significantly better than LLM-Empirical (p<1e-4). Mutation score 0.980/0.939/0.937 beats EvoSuite by at least 0.049 (all p<1e-4). Oracles: 0.910/0.930/0.894 on correct code and 0.904/0.911/0.873 on faulty code, outperforming fine-tuned TOGLL by at least 21.1 percentage points (A12 = 0.920 correct, 0.960 faulty). Ablations: removing Planner drops line/branch/mutation by at least 0.050/0.046/0.070; removing the panel drops oracle correctness by 0.067-0.086; replacing panel with majority voting still loses at least 0.014. Panelists disagreed in over 70% of discussions, and the Curator cross-checks reasoning rather than voting. Single-LLM role blending produced concrete syntax errors (Python-style [1] instead of Arrays.asList(1)).
extraction.limitations: Construct: no real-bug detection on project-level datasets such as Defects4J; mutation score is used as a bug-finding proxy. Internal: results depend on LLaMA 3.1 70B and DeepSeek R1 only, and benchmark data may be present in pretraining corpora (mitigated via mutants). External: only two datasets, both without user-defined or external class dependencies, so generalisation to complex real projects is unestablished; a dependency-resolution agent is left to future work. records.title: Towards Engineering Multi-Agent LLMs: A Protocol-Driven Approach

evidence_notes.finding: SEMAP treats multi-agent LLM failure as a classical software-engineering design defect (missing contracts, untyped interfaces, ungated transitions) and shows that adding behavioural contracts, typed messaging, and verification-gated lifecycle FSMs cuts MAST-classified failures by up to 69.6% on function-level development and 47.4% on Python vulnerability detection relative to a MetaGPT baseline.
evidence_notes.quote: Despite their conceptual appeal, current multi-agent LLM systems often under-perform in practice, as evidenced by high failure rates on SE tasks.

extraction.framework: SEMAP (Software Engineering Multi-Agent Protocol), protocol middleware over Google Agent-to-Agent (A2A); baseline built on MetaGPT
extraction.agent_count: 5 for development (CEO, Planner, Coder, Reviewer, Tester); 3 for vulnerability detection (Auditor, Critic, Tester)
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval (function-level), ProgramDev (deployment-level), devign100 (C/C++ vulnerability), vudenc100 (Python vulnerability from CVEFixes); failures classified by the MAST LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline using gpt-4o-2024-08-06
extraction.baseline: MetaGPT multi-agent baseline without the protocol layer (same agent roles, same models: DeepSeek-V3-0324 and gpt-4.1-nano)
extraction.key_results: HumanEval total failures fell 64.1% with ChatGPT (256->92) and 69.6% with DeepSeek (112->34), with under-specification down 71.5% and 73.0%. ProgramDev fell 12.6% (103->90) and 56.7% (67->29), with inter-agent misalignment eliminated entirely for DeepSeek. devign100 fell 28.2% (78->56) and 8.3% (48->44); vudenc100 fell 47.4% (38->20) and 16.4% (55->46). Round-wise, SEMAP under-specification failures dropped from 20 to 2 (ChatGPT) and 14 to 0 (DeepSeek) by round 5, while baseline failures declined more slowly and reappeared after temporary drops.
extraction.limitations: Explicitly a preliminary evaluation. No single-agent LLM baseline and no domain-specific detector baseline were run (both deferred to future work), so the study cannot speak to multi-agent versus single-agent parity. No ablation isolating contracts, messaging, or lifecycle control. Resource overhead is unmeasured. Small datasets (100-sample vulnerability subsets), few collaboration rounds (5), two models, and reliance on an LLM-as-a-Judge failure classifier. Formal protocol correctness verification and artifact release are listed as future work.

records.title: Methods and Techniques of Agentic Software Engineering: A Systematic Literature Review

evidence_notes.finding: This SLR of 61 studies (2022-2025) documents a field-wide migration from single-agent to role-specialized multi-agent architectures and asserts reliability and performance gains, but its own challenge analysis reports that inter-agent protocols are informal and non-standardised, conflict resolution is immature, and token cost scales disproportionately with system complexity.
evidence_notes.quote: The complexity of a multi-agent system increases its computational costs disproportionately with the complexity of the system since multiple agents take a much larger number of tokens to interact with each other and require more processing time, which may render large-scale implementation uneconomical in practice.

extraction.benchmark: Reports benchmark usage across the corpus rather than running one: 67% of studies use established benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-bench), 43% build domain-specific tasks, 29% add human evaluation, 18% report real-world deployment case studies
extraction.key_results: 61 primary studies from 2022-2025. Mean agent autonomy rating rose from 2.3 (2022) to 3.8 (2024) on a 4-point scale, with top-autonomy studies rising from 18% to 73%. Metrics: pass@k in 89% of code generation studies, task completion rate in 76% of multi-agent studies, human preference scores in 63% of human-agent studies, cost-effectiveness in only 41%. Claims multi-agent decomposition 'increases performance and reliability over single-agent monolithic systems' and that tool-augmented, environment-aware agents outperform isolated agents. Of the 29 studies reporting industrial adoption, trust and reliability was the top barrier (78%), then legacy integration (64%), absent standardised evaluation metrics (59%), and skills gaps (52%). Practitioner guidance is to start with single-agent tools before adopting multi-agent systems.
extraction.limitations: Self-reported threats: selection bias from a fast-moving field and possibly missed preprints; subjective quality assessment and extraction inconsistency; publication bias toward positive results; 2022-2025 temporal scope; English-only; inconsistent definitions of 'agentic'; heterogeneous evaluation metrics preventing direct cross-study comparison; limited long-term deployment data; and only 61 studies, leaving thin coverage in subcategories. The claimed multi-agent superiority is a narrative synthesis, not a controlled comparison. The review also cites evidence that semantically equivalent natural-language task phrasings yield dissimilar implementations, and that long-term maintainability of agent-written code is essentially unstudied.

records.title: From benchmarks to deployment: a comprehensive review of agentic AI evaluation

evidence_notes.finding: A critical review of 15 agent benchmarks finds evaluation methodology, not model capability, is the binding constraint on deployment: 0/15 score safety or security, 0/15 include cost-efficiency in the primary protocol, 13/15 rely solely on binary success, and no benchmark exceeds 50% on the authors' deployment-readiness rubric.
evidence_notes.quote: Multi-agent systems bring about coordination failures, emergent behavior and dynamics of interaction that cannot be seen in single-agent benchmarks.

extraction.benchmark: Analyses 15 benchmarks: AgentBench, WebArena, SWE-bench, PaperBench, MLGym, BrowserGym, HumanEval, MBPP, GAIA, ToolBench, Terminal-Bench, Mind2Web, ALFWorld, BabyAI, HotPotQA
extraction.key_results: 0/15 benchmarks integrate safety or security into scoring; 0/15 penalise unsafe tool usage; 0/15 systematically test adversarial robustness; 0/15 include cost-efficiency in the primary protocol; 13/15 use binary success as the sole criterion; trajectory quality is unmeasured in 14/15. Gap scores: SWE-bench 20%, ALFWorld 35%, WebArena 45%. Across 1,240 agent trajectories, action efficiency varied 340% (mean 12.4 steps, SD 42.1) among agents with identical 80% success rates, yet current metrics assign identical scores. Explicitly notes that architecturally distinct systems (ReAct, Reflexion, multi-agent frameworks) have radically different failure modes that architecture-agnostic benchmarks cannot distinguish, and that existing frameworks have weak infrastructure for multi-agent robustness or cooperative safety.
extraction.limitations: Narrative critical review rather than a protocol-registered systematic review; the deployment-readiness rubric and gap-scoring framework are authored by the reviewers and not externally validated. No new experiments are run and no dataset was generated. The paper itself flags unresolved barriers to its recommended paradigms: high computational and monetary cost of trajectory-level evaluation, irreproducibility in stochastic interactive environments, the contextual and low-probability nature of safety making it hard to standardise, the unresolved realism-versus-control tension, and continued benchmark overfitting and leaderboard gaming.

records.title: Evaluating large language model agents for automation of atomic force microscopy

evidence_notes.finding: On AFMBench the multi-agent AILA configuration beat direct single-agent tool integration for GPT-4o (70% vs 58% success) but made no measurable difference for weaker models, and the authors document 'sleepwalking', where agents take unauthorised actions beyond their instructions, as a distinct instruction-adherence failure mode separate from code-generation errors.
evidence_notes.quote: In one of the four recorded errors, GPT-4o exceeded its designated operational limits, performing actions that were not authorized by the provided guidelines.

extraction.framework: AILA (Artificially Intelligent Lab Assistant): LLM planner with dynamic routing over an AFM Handler Agent and a Data Handler Agent, plus document-retrieval, code-execution, Image Optimizer, and Image Analyzer tools
extraction.agent_count: 2 specialized agents plus a planner (3 total)
extraction.benchmark: AFMBench (100 tasks x 3 trials = 300 instances spanning workflow design, multi-tool coordination, decision-making, open-ended experiments, and data analysis), plus five real AFM experiments
extraction.baseline: Single-agent AILA with direct tool integration, evaluated on a 10-question AFMBench subset with 3 trials each; also cross-model comparison of GPT-4o, GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, Llama-3.3-70B-versatile, Claude-3.5-sonnet
extraction.key_results: Multi-agent GPT-4o reached 70% success vs 58% for direct tool integration; for the other models the difference was minimal because they failed at cross-domain tasks regardless of topology. Overall task success: GPT-4o 65%, GPT-3.5 32.8%. Total error rates: GPT-4o 29% (code generation 21.7%, instruction adherence 5.7%, agent selection 1.3%, tool selection 0.3%), GPT-3.5 66.6%, Llama-3.3-70B 60.6%, Claude-3.5 51.6% (dominated by 28.3% agent-selection errors misrouting between the AFM and Data handlers). GPT-4o used about 2.5 agent calls per AFM Handler task; Claude-3.5 had the highest mean latency (17.31 s) and most verbose outputs, Llama-3.3-70B the lowest (7 s). Debugging capped at 20 iterations, with failures split into iteration-limit exhaustion and sleepwalking. Materials-science question-answering skill did not predict laboratory performance.
extraction.limitations: Single instrument domain (atomic force microscopy) and a single framework, so generalisation across scientific platforms is asserted rather than demonstrated. The single-versus-multi-agent comparison uses only 10 of the benchmark questions with 3 trials each, and the advantage appears for one model only. Both architectures remain fragile to minor changes in instruction formatting or prompting. Persistent code-generation errors occur despite direct access to documentation and snippets, indicating limits of the retrieval-augmented setup. Sleepwalking raises unresolved safety-alignment risks for autonomous laboratories, and the authors call for domain-specific constraint validation and formal verification that the system does not yet have.

records.title: Beyond Task Completion: An Assessment Framework for Evaluating Agentic AI Systems

evidence_notes.finding: In a production CloudOps deployment, binary task-completion metrics were identical between baseline and framework evaluation while pillar-specific metrics exposed substantial hidden behavioural failures (S1 had 100% tool sequencing but 33% policy adherence; S2 completed the task with 13.1% memory recall), and the multi-agent scenario S3 had by far the worst tool-orchestration failure rate (7.67 average failures) and the only environment guardrail violations.
evidence_notes.quote: Memory failures increased with scenario complexity, while Environment violations appeared only in multi-agent scenarios where production states changed despite guardrails.

extraction.framework: Agent Assessment Framework (four pillars: LLM, Memory, Tools, Environment) applied to MOYA multi-agent framework with Mem0 memory and ChromaDB, in collaboration with MontyCloud Inc.
extraction.agent_count: 5 agents across three scenarios (Cost, Security, Performance, Remediation, RCA)
extraction.benchmark: Three production-motivated Autonomous CloudOps scenarios (S1 cost optimization, S2 security incident response, S3 multi-agent root cause analysis), 3 independent runs each; GPT-4o at temperature 0.7
extraction.baseline: Conventional baseline evaluation capturing only task completion and tool usage ratio, compared against deterministic pillar metrics plus LLM-as-Judge and Agent-as-Judge protocols
extraction.key_results: Baseline and framework report identical task completion (S1 0%, S2 100%, S3 33%) and tool usage (0.80/0.97/0.62), but framework-only metrics reveal policy adherence of 33%/100%/0%, tool sequence correctness of 100%/33%/53%, and memory F1 of 31.1%/18.1%/51.32%. Memory decomposition for S3: single-hop P/R 63.3/61.1, multi-hop 100.0/26.5, temporal 100.0/29.8 (high precision, poor recall). Pillar failure averages show Tools worst in S3 (7.67), Memory rising 0.67 -> 2.33 -> 3.67 with complexity, and Environment guardrail violations only in S3 (2.00). Agent-as-Judge caught the Remediation Agent skipping a pre-policy check (4/5) and the Performance Agent missing a configuration lookup (9/10). Cost: scenario execution averaged $0.0621 and 183.5 s; LLM-as-Judge added $0.0593 and 14.7 s, whereas Agent-as-Judge cost $0.9572 and 913.4 s, i.e. 16x cost and 62x time, with S3 alone accounting for $0.6110 due to multi-agent verification cycles.

Internal: single model (GPT-4o) and a fixed temperature of 0.7 may not span the non-determinism distribution; author-defined ground-truth contracts may exclude valid solution paths; judge-based protocols carry LLM evaluation bias. Construct: metrics may miss reliability aspects, memory assessment excludes storage efficiency and concurrent access, and environment checks cannot measure observability quality or recovery because the environment is textually simulated. Expected behaviours were specified manually.

records.title: Small LLMs Are Weak Tool Learners: A Multi-LLM Agent

extraction.framework: alpha-UMi (multi-LLM agent: planner, caller, summarizer) trained with global-to-local progressive fine-tuning (GLPFT) on LLaMA-2-chat 7B/13B
extraction.agent_count: 3 (planner, caller, summarizer)
extraction.benchmark: ToolBench (in-domain and out-of-domain step-wise metrics plus real-time RapidAPI ToolEval), ToolAlpaca, and program-aided mathematical reasoning (GSM8K/MATH) in the appendix
extraction.baseline: Single-LLM, Multi-LLM one-stage, Single-LLM multi-task, ToolLLaMA, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Claude-2; LoRA variants
extraction.key_results: 7B alpha-UMi w/ reuse reaches Plan ACC 88.92 / Act. EM 58.94 / Hallu. 0.57 / Arg. F1 52.24 in-domain versus Single-LLM 81.92 / 53.26 / 2.32 / 45.57; out-of-domain 89.72 / 60.47 / 0.45 / 53.60 versus 84.61 / 56.54 / 2.26 / 50.09. 7B alpha-UMi beats the 13B Single-LLM baseline. 13B alpha-UMi reaches Plan ACC 87.87, Act. EM 63.03, Hallu. 0.37, Arg. F1 57.65. Real-time ToolEval: alpha-UMi 7B averages 70.9 pass / 65.9 win, beating GPT-3.5 (+6.1 pass, +1.6 win) and ToolLLaMA (+10.2, +5.9), and matching or exceeding GPT-4 pass rate on I1-Inst. and I2-Inst. while trailing GPT-4 on win rate (71.1 / 70.4). records.title: Triangle: Empowering Incident Triage with Multi-Agent

evidence_notes.finding: In a production cloud deployment, Triangle's multi-role negotiation is the single most load-bearing component: removing multi-agent negotiation costs about 12 points of hop-1 accuracy (54.7% -> 42.8%) and 21 points at hop 5 (91.7% -> 70.4%), more than removing semantic distillation, while automated team-information enrichment matters most at higher hop counts.
evidence_notes.quote: The most substantial performance degradation is observed when the multi-agent negotiation mechanism is removed(w/o MAT).

extraction.framework: TRIANGLE (Analyzer Agent, Triage Decider Agent, Team Manager Agents) with semantic distillation, majority-vote negotiation, and automated Team Information Enrichment
extraction.agent_count: 3 agent types; one Team Manager Agent per organisational team, so the negotiating population scales with candidate teams
extraction.benchmark: Real-world production incident data from a global cloud provider (hop accuracy at hops 1-5 across nine services, plus six deployed services measured 3 months pre/post) and the public MSR 2013 Bug Dataset
extraction.baseline: DeepCT (state of the art), plus ContentBased, InvertedIndex, LGBM, and MART from DeepTriage; ablations w/o semantic distillation, w/o multi-agent negotiation, w/o team information enrichment
extraction.key_results: Hop accuracy 54.7 / 70.4 / 80.5 / 86.0 / 91.7 versus DeepCT 43.4 / 54.6 / 60.4 / 64.4 / 67.6, a 26-42% relative improvement, achieved without manually enriched discussions that DeepCT requires. Deployed triage accuracy up to 97% (Teams C/E/F 96-97%, A 92%, B 82%, D 64%) and TTE reductions of 18-91% across six services. Ablations at hop 1 / hop 5: w/o negotiation 42.8 / 70.4, w/o semantic distillation 49.1 / 86.1, w/o team information enrichment 49.6 / 65.8 versus full 54.7 / 91.7. Generalises to MSR 2013 bug triage at 63.2% accuracy, beating baselines by 15.3-134.9%. Operates on roughly 600 million logs and 20 TB per day across over 2,000 fault types. No contemporary single-agent LLM baseline was run; the authors justify the omission by citing prior work rather than by experiment, which leaves the multi-agent advantage over a strong single-prompt LLM unmeasured. Absolute incident volumes are withheld as confidential.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 1,026 manually annotated bugs in LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Haystack, agent orchestration frameworks depart from traditional software bug profiles: Incorrect Functionality (315) nearly matches Crash (326), a new Unexpected Output category accounts for 16.5%, and the authors conclude that deterministic testing and static analysis are structurally inadequate for these probabilistic, heavily integrated systems.

extraction.baseline: Comparison against bug-characterisation patterns reported for traditional and deep-learning software systems
extraction.key_results: 1,026 bug instances extracted from 1,577 manually annotated bug-related GitHub pull requests, classified into nine root causes and six symptoms. Root causes: code logic errors 38.0% (390) and API misuse about 24.7-24.8% (254) dominate, with parameter/argument issues 15.6% (160) and incompatibility 5.5% (56). Symptoms: Crash 31.8% (326), Incorrect Functionality 30.7% (315), Unexpected Output 16.5% (169), External Connection Failure (103), Hang, Unidentified. Component skew: Agent Construction has 16.0% incompatibility (about triple the overall rate) and elevated incorrect exception handling (6.0%); Featured Modules reach 48.3% code logic issues; core schema components concentrate parameter validation issues. Parameter/argument issues frequently cascade into external connection failures. Conclusion: conventional testing presupposes deterministic outcomes in discrete state spaces while these frameworks operate over continuous probability distributions with non-linear compositional effects, motivating metamorphic oracles and framework-cognisant static analysis.

Manual labelling of root causes and symptoms depends on subjective interpretation and can introduce bias. Only three frameworks were analysed, restricting generalisability to other architectures and use cases. The study characterises bugs in the orchestration frameworks themselves rather than in the multi-agent applications built on them, and it does not measure downstream impact on agent task success. records.title: Large Language Model-Based Agents for Software Engineering: A Survey

evidence_notes.finding: Surveying 124 papers, this review classifies multi-agent SE collaboration into layered, circular, star-like, tree-like, and mesh structures with unidirectional-transfer or bidirectional-chat information flow, and reports that all of these structures hit performance bottlenecks as agent count grows, with prior work showing benchmark performance saturating regardless of collaboration structure.
evidence_notes.quote: The collaboration structures mentioned above may all encounter performance bottlenecks as the scale increases.

extraction.agent_count: Varies across the corpus; systems typically fix agent count to task scale, e.g. AutoAgents and AgentVerse cap derivation at four agents, SoA limits tree depth to 2, and MAGIS derives developer agents from the number of suspicious files (SWE-bench average 1.7)
extraction.benchmark: Discusses SWE-bench, HumanEval, MMLU and others as used across the surveyed corpus rather than running an evaluation
extraction.baseline: Contrasts multi-agent collaboration against tool-enhanced single-agent strategies within surveyed tasks; of 50 single-agent works collected, only 12 assign an explicit role, and those roles are all covered by the multi-agent role taxonomy
extraction.key_results: 124 papers categorised from SE and agent perspectives. Collaboration mechanisms: layered (sequential pipeline, sometimes with parallel same-layer voting such as AgentForest and DyLAN), circular (dual-role generation-validation loops such as INTERVENOR, and multi-role reflection loops such as DroidAgent), star-like (RCAgent, AutoGen, XUAT-Copilot, AutoDev scheduler), tree-like (SoA spawning mother/child agents), and mesh (3DGen group chat, MacNet). Information flow is either unidirectional transfer, the most common pattern because it preserves per-agent context and enables decoupling, or bidirectional chat over a shared dialogue history; ChatDev combines both. Requirements engineering comparison: multi-agent role-play broadens phase coverage but introduces quality-assurance problems in collaborative settings, whereas tool-enhanced single-agent methods yield higher-quality artefacts at the cost of task scalability (SpecGen with OpenJML outperforms purely LLM-based methods by 15.84%). Only 46.7% of surveyed papers quantify efficiency (time, token consumption, monetary cost, tool or inter-agent discussion frequency).
extraction.limitations: As a survey it runs no controlled comparisons, so relative multi-agent versus single-agent effectiveness is synthesised from heterogeneous primary studies. The authors identify field-level gaps as open problems: evaluations are coarse black-box success rates without intermediate-state or per-module metrics, so failure causes cannot be attributed; robustness, security, and fairness are underexplored relative to effectiveness; cost is largely unreported; SWE-bench contains vague or incomplete issue descriptions and 77.8% of its tasks are completable by an experienced engineer within an hour; and end-to-end generated software is typically a single function or a few files, far below real-project complexity. Human-agent interaction is confined to a few phases, and perception is mostly textual or visual.

records.title: Multi-Agent Assisted Automatic Test Generation for Java JSON Libraries

evidence_notes.finding: JSONATG's three-role decomposition (Code Summarizer, Test Programmer, Test Validator) with domain-specific mutation rules outperformed ChatTester and ChatUnitest on the large, complex fastjson classes and found 59 real bugs for $25, but the ablation shows the agent-written mutation rules actually reduced coverage on four of six classes because more generated tests failed to compile, and the Test Validator was near chance at classifying tests that throw library-defined exceptions.
evidence_notes.quote: JSONATG achieves higher coverage on complex and large classes in the Java JSON library, demonstrating superior capability in exercising critical components of the library under test.

extraction.framework: JSONATG (code summarization agent, Test Programmer, Test Validator) with agent-generated JSON-domain program mutation rules and post-processing
extraction.benchmark: Instruction coverage over six core fastjson classes (JSON, JSONPath, JSONArray, JSONObject, JSONReader, JSONWriter) seeded with historical bug-triggering unit tests, plus real bug reporting against fastjson
extraction.baseline: ChatTester and ChatUnitest (both LLM-based, GPT-3.5); internal ablations against free mutation, no test-intention summarization, and alternative LLMs (Llama3, DeepSeek-coder-6.7B, GPT-3.5)
extraction.key_results: JSONATG wins on JSON (32.76 vs 6.50/2.39), JSONPath (20.46 vs 11.16/0.33), JSONReader (44.86 vs 4.85/1.88), and JSONWriter (41.88 vs 4.64/2.68), but loses on the getter-heavy JSONArray (29.64 vs 52.51) and JSONObject (41.33 vs 47.47). Baselines fail on large classes because including focal-method source exceeds the token limit. With a $25 budget and about 40 CPU hours, 59 bugs were reported in fastjson, 47 confirmed and 28 fixed. Ablation: free mutation beats agent-written mutation on four of six classes because agent-rule tests compile less often, yet each rule set found unique bugs (5 unique free, 4 unique agent-written, 3 shared). Removing intention summarization raised compile errors from 13.9% to 25.7% and lowered pass rate from 56.3% to 54.2%. Of compiled tests, 67.0% pass, 25.6% fail on assertions, 7.4% crash. Test Validator averaged 72.1% accuracy few-shot and 69.8% with chain-of-thought, strong on assertion failures (10/11, 10/12) but near chance on exception-throwing cases (7/10, 4/10). Model comparison: GPT-3.5 best overall, Llama3 worst with a 25.71% compile-error rate versus 12.73% for DeepSeek, and all three surfaced distinct bugs.
extraction.limitations: Authors' threats: inherent randomness of LLM agent outputs, mitigated only by fixing temperature and top-p and pinning model versions; the design assumes JSON-P and JSON-B standards apply to the library under test, which may not hold universally. Stated limitations: many generated tests remain uncompiled and are discarded, wasting budget and losing potentially valuable tests; Test Validator false positives forced reliance on a differential oracle between fastjson2 and fastjson, which requires two implementations of the same specification and does not generalise. Evaluation is confined to one library (fastjson) and six classes, coverage is instruction-level only, and no traditional search-based or fuzzing baseline is included.

extraction.agent_count: 1 supervisor agent plus multiple specialist agents, with hierarchy depth greater than one
