evidence_notes.finding: Across 120 trajectories and 2,822 LLM interactions from three single-agent SE systems, failed runs are distinguished by repetitive non-adaptive action cycles, result-insensitive next actions, and rare but costly thought-action misalignments; even a single misalignment correlated with failure or greatly increased cost (one bug extended from iteration 6 to iteration 38).
evidence_notes.quote: Repetition wastes iterations and may induce unproductive loops, as also observed in RQ2.

extraction.agent_count: single-agent systems; 3 distinct agents studied, 40 trajectories each
extraction.benchmark: Defects4J (RepairAgent) and SWE-bench Lite (AutoCodeRover, OpenHands); 120 trajectories, 2,822 LLM interactions
extraction.baseline: successful vs failed trajectories within and across the three agents

extraction.agent_count: 2-3 LLM agents (Analyst, Coder, Tester) with up to 3 collaboration iterations
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval and HumanEval+ (pass@1), evaluated over 19 LLMs
extraction.baseline: Basic one-shot prompting, AC (Analyst-Coder), ACT, Debugger only, and AC + Debugger
extraction.key_results: HumanEval mean accuracy: ACT+Debug 64.82%, Debug alone 63.86%, ACT alone 57.16%, Basic 56.48%. ACT+Debug significantly beats ACT but not Debug alone (+0.96%, not significant at alpha=0.15). Gains from chaining are largest when the two techniques perform comparably. Robustness drop from HumanEval to HumanEval+: Basic 90.83, Debugger only 107.84, AC+Debugger 110.41, ACT 118.51, AC 129.27, ACT+Debugger 137.74. records.title: Demystifying LLM-Based Software Engineering Agents: A Review of Capabilities, Benchmarks, and Failure Modes

evidence_notes.finding: A critical review of 20+ primary studies frames an 'Agentless Paradox': structured non-agentic pipelines match or beat autonomous single- and multi-agent systems on SWE-bench at up to an order of magnitude lower cost (Agentless 1.0 27.3% at $0.34/issue vs SWE-search MCTS 23.0% at ~$4.00), and base-model choice explains more variance than architecture; the review also warns that multi-agent debate reinforces rather than corrects correlated errors when all agents share one base model.
evidence_notes.quote: When many agents make the same mistake, we call it a correlated error.

extraction.benchmark: reviewed benchmarks: HumanEval, MBPP, AgentBench, SWE-bench / Lite / Verified, Multi-SWE-bench, TheAgentCompany, SWE-bench Pro
extraction.baseline: Agentless structured pipelines and RAG baselines compared against single-agent ReAct, multi-agent collaborative, AST-augmented, MCTS-enhanced, and open-platform agents
extraction.key_results: Six architectural classes compared. Resolution rates rose from under 5% at SWE-bench's 2023 launch to over 75% on SWE-bench Verified by 2025. Agentless 1.0 (27.3% Lite, $0.34/issue) beat SWE-search (23.0%, ~$4.00) by 4.3 points at ~12x lower cost; swapping GPT-4o for Claude 3.5 Sonnet inside Agentless lifted Lite resolution from 27.3% to 40.7% (49% relative), attributing gains to the model rather than the architecture. Cost per resolved issue spans $0.34 to $10+ for similar accuracy. Six failure modes with prevalence and mitigation effectiveness: hallucination (very high), context overflow (high), test overfitting (high), over-engineering (medium), inter-agent errors (medium), security boundary violations (low-medium).
extraction.limitations: A narrative critical review of more than 20 primary studies rather than a systematic meta-analysis, with rounded or estimated per-issue costs; the review itself flags unresolved ecological validity, temporal data leakage from pre-training corpora, benchmark saturation at the high end, adversarial robustness, and safety auditing as open gaps; resolution rate as a metric hides test overfitting and regression-inducing patches.

records.title: Developing LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems in Software Engineering: A Mixed-Method Experience Report

extraction.benchmark: GitHub README.MD summarization with prompt-optimization datasets TS_10 and TS_50, scored with ROUGE-1/2/L and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests
extraction.baseline: cross-framework comparison; no single-agent baseline
extraction.key_results: Mean ROUGE on TS_10: Dify 0.515/0.352/0.479, Semantic Kernel 0.505/0.344/0.472, AutoGen 0.488/0.294/0.441, AutoGPT 0.473/0.275/0.428, Semantic Kernel Chat 0.472/0.278/0.427; Dify and Semantic Kernel are statistically indistinguishable (p>0.05). Frameworks cover coordination rules, role/behaviour specification, and message handling, but lack benchmarking, monitoring/telemetry, and human-in-the-loop integration. Lessons learned: monitoring capabilities are in their infancy, agent communication protocols (MCP, A2A) are crucial, empirical MAS metrics are missing, and VectorDB is the common long-term memory solution. Challenges: tool incompleteness (notably AutoGPT documentation and bugs) and limited low-code frameworks.
extraction.limitations: Qualitative assessment rests on the authors' subjective experience and may be biased; only a limited number of frameworks were analysed, restricting generalization; task-specific analysis covered a single optimization/summarization task; only one model provider (OpenAI) was used; ROUGE metrics may not adequately capture MAS performance; industrially adopted but unpublished frameworks were excluded.

records.title: CAPRA: Scaling Feedback on Software Architecture Deliverables with a Multi-Agent LLM System

evidence_notes.finding: Adding a deterministic Evidence Anchoring step (normalized Levenshtein fuzzy matching) plus a ConsistencyManager agent to a multi-agent LLM reviewer let CAPRA satisfy 88.8% of eight rubric criteria under strict two-rater aggregation, but reliability collapsed on the interpretive 'Grounded Issues' criterion (50% strict pass, kappa 0.348), so human oversight remains necessary for subjective dimensions.
evidence_notes.quote: Importantly, the Evidence Anchoring mechanism acted as a verification gate: findings that could not be verified against the source text were filtered out, substantially reducing ungrounded critiques.

extraction.framework: CAPRA (Configurable Architecture Proficiency Report Assessment) with gpt-4o vision extraction and gpt-5.1 analysis agents
extraction.agent_count: multiple specialized agents (multi-modal extraction, dimension-specific analyzers, ConsistencyManager); exact count not stated
extraction.benchmark: custom eight-criterion binary rubric (A1-D1) applied by two human raters to 10 student software-architecture reports, plus 10 separate reports for knowledge-base construction
extraction.baseline: manual instructor review estimated at 30-45 minutes per report
extraction.key_results: 88.8% criteria pass under strict (min of two raters) aggregation and 91.9% lenient; raw inter-rater agreement 93.75% over 80 decisions with Cohen's kappa 0.582 (moderate). Perfect 100% pass on use-case completeness, test types/coverage, feature validation, and actionable recommendations; weakest on Grounded Issues (65% lenient, 50% strict, kappa 0.348) and Architecture & Design Patterns (85%/80%, kappa 0.615). Mean processing 248s (SD 73.1s) at about $0.44 per report, a 7.2-10.8x speedup over manual review. The knowledge base was auto-generated from 680 raw mentions via HDBSCAN clustering with no manual rubric authoring.
extraction.limitations: Both raters were paper authors, risking evaluator bias; only top-scoring reports were used, inflating pass rates and never stressing the system with deficient deliverables; 10 reports from one course at one university; a single proprietary model (gpt-5.1) creates cost and reproducibility dependencies and residual non-determinism; binary Pass/Fail rubric loses granularity; Evidence Anchoring thresholds were set empirically without sensitivity analysis; observed cross-lingual drift where Italian source documents caused mixed-language output.

records.title: AgentNet: Decentralized Evolutionary Coordination for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_notes.finding: A decentralized DAG-structured framework with retrieval-augmented agent evolution outperformed centralized multi-agent baselines such as MetaGPT and GPTSwarm and matched or beat strong single-agent prompting, but the heterogeneity ablation showed role/model diversity actually hurts small teams and only pays off at larger scale, and several multi-agent baselines fell far below single-agent prompting.
evidence_notes.quote: With 3 agents, the fully homogeneous setting performs best, while introducing either model or skill diversity reduces accuracy, suggesting uniform reasoning is more effective in small teams.

extraction.framework: AgentNet, a decentralized RAG-based DAG framework with dynamic routing and adaptive expertise evolution
extraction.agent_count: 3 agents in the main comparison; scaling experiments with 3, 5, 7, and 9 agents
extraction.benchmark: MATH (140 test problems), BBH (100 test problems), API-Bank function calling (100 test tasks)
extraction.baseline: single-agent: Direct, ReAct, Synapse, Self-Consistency, Self-Refinement; multi-agent: MorphAgent, MetaGPT, AFLOW, GPTSwarm
extraction.key_results: DeepSeek-V3 backbone: AgentNet 92.86 MATH / 94.00 BBH / 30.00 API-Bank, best or second in every column; centralized MetaGPT reached only 64.00 BBH (DeepSeek-V3) and 53.00 (GPT-4o-mini). Several multi-agent baselines underperform single-agent prompting (MorphAgent 39.29 MATH vs Synapse 89.28 on DeepSeek-V3). Router ablation: 82.14% training / 86.00% test accuracy on BBH, above randomized routing variants. Removing the evolution phase drops MATH 85.00 to 77.86, API-Bank 32.00 to 23.00, BBH 86.00 to 76.00. Heterogeneity hurts at 3 agents (0.86 homogeneous vs 0.81 both-hetero) but helps at 5 agents (0.79 vs 0.85). Scaling from 3 agents/30 executors to 9 agents/40 executors gives only 80.38 to 81.18 training accuracy (diminishing returns).
extraction.limitations: Performance under heterogeneous agent capabilities, workflows, tools, and data remains an open question and may introduce coordination overhead; the router selects from a relatively small predefined candidate pool and its behaviour at hundreds or thousands of agents is unstudied; incentives for exploring agents beyond the predefined set are future work; no software-engineering benchmark is evaluated.

records.title: Large language model-based multi-agent systems for automated foundation design: router-driven task classification and expert selection framework

evidence_notes.finding: Router-driven dispatch to domain-expert agents beat both a single strong agent (95.00% vs 86.25% shallow foundations; 90.63% vs 87.50% pile design with Grok 3) and conventional fixed designer-checker multi-agent workflows by 10.0-43.75 points, while the fixed sequential multi-agent workflows actually underperformed the plain single agent, and the router configuration also had the lowest run-to-run variance.
evidence_notes.quote: Perfect scores (100.00%) consistently showed zero standard deviation, suggesting deterministic reasoning paths when models achieve complete problem understanding despite the probabilistic generation process.

extraction.framework: router-based multi-agent framework with dual-tier task classification and specialized domain-expert agents (Grok 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro backbones)
extraction.agent_count: 1 router plus specialized expert agents; the compared designer-checker workflows use 2 agents
extraction.benchmark: 27 foundation-design test cases across seven categories (shallow foundation and pile design), each executed in triple trials
extraction.baseline: single-agent processing with DeepSeek R1, ChatGPT 4 Turbo, Grok 3, and Gemini 2.5 Pro; conventional Agentic Workflow I and II (designer-checker)
extraction.key_results: Router workflow with Grok 3: 95.00% shallow foundation and 90.63% pile design, +8.75 and +3.13 points over standalone Grok 3 (86.25% / 87.50%) and 10.0-43.75 points over conventional workflows. With Gemini 2.5 Pro: 82.50% and 84.38%. Conventional Agentic Workflow I underperformed even single agents (38.75% shallow with Gemini 2.5 Pro; 51.56% pile). Router configuration achieved the lowest variance (SD 1.73% shallow, 3.25% pile) while weak configurations exceeded 8.0% SD. Perfect 100% performance on Pile Group analysis with both backbones vs 50.00-68.75% for conventional workflows.
extraction.limitations: Only 27 test cases across seven categories, giving limited statistical power (standard error roughly +/-4-6 points, so differences must exceed about 8-10 points to be reliable); results are presented as preliminary and needing validation on 100+ cases and independent replication; scope limited to shallow and pile foundations, excluding mat foundations, combined footings, and pile-raft systems; safety-critical use still requires continued human oversight.

records.title: Automated Summarization of Software Documents: An LLM-based Multi-Agent Approach

evidence_notes.finding: A four-agent teacher-student prompt-refinement system consistently outperformed single-LLM baselines (Mixtral-8x7B, Llama-2-7b, GPT-4o, Gemma-2-2b) on ROUGE and cosine similarity for software document summarization, and an adaptive stopping strategy cut training from 620 to 260 iterations with comparable quality, though the authors note multi-agent orchestration still adds computational overhead.
evidence_notes.quote: Despite the efficiency gains achieved by the dynamic iteration strategy, the orchestration of multiple LLM-based agents inevitably introduces computational overhead.

extraction.framework: Metagente, an LLM-based multi-agent system with a Teacher-Student prompt-optimization loop and dynamic stopping
extraction.agent_count: 4 LLM-based agents (including Summarizer Agent and Teacher Agent)
extraction.benchmark: GitHub README-to-About summarization and Google Play HTML app-description summarization datasets (D1, D2), scored with ROUGE-1/2/L and cosine similarity
extraction.baseline: single-agent LLMs Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1, Llama-2-7b-hf, GPT-4o, and Gemma-2-2b-it; earlier GitSum (BART/T5)
extraction.key_results: Metagente consistently outperforms all single-agent baselines across ROUGE and cosine similarity on both datasets; Metagente ROUGE-L mostly ranges 0.3-1.0 on D1 while Mixtral and Llama-2-7b stay below 0.2, and Mixtral's ROUGE scores are mostly under 0.15 with high variance. The dynamic iteration strategy converged in 260 iterations versus 620 for the non-dynamic variant with comparable ROUGE and stronger cosine similarity, while reducing flow duration, step duration, and input/output token counts.
extraction.limitations: Evaluation limited to GitHub README and Google Play descriptions in English, so generalization to requirement specifications, technical reports, or bug reports is untested; ROUGE and cosine similarity may not capture semantic fidelity, factual consistency, or user-perceived usefulness; Google Play 'About' ground truth is marketing-oriented; possible overlap with LLM pre-training corpora could inflate results; Teacher-Student loop is sensitive to iteration thresholds and ROUGE cutoffs; single-agent baselines are sensitive to prompt and hyperparameter setup, affecting comparison fairness; multi-agent orchestration adds computational cost at scale.

records.title: A Systematic Survey of LLM-Based Agentic AI Frameworks for Multi-Agent Coordination and Interoperability

evidence_notes.finding: A PRISMA review of 121 studies concludes that the binding constraints on LLM multi-agent systems are architectural rather than model-level: evaluation standardization, long-horizon reliability, communication security, interoperability, cost-efficient orchestration, governance, and system-level interpretability. It argues agent systems must be evaluated as holistic architectures rather than by benchmarking the base LLM in isolation.
evidence_notes.quote:
The literature review suggests that these challenges are beyond 
the capabilities of individual language models and include evaluation standardization, long -horizon reliability, 
security, interoperability, communication efficiency, governance, and interpretability.

extraction.framework: LangChain/LangGraph, AutoGPT, AutoGen, MetaGPT, CAMEL, ChatDev, CrewAI (surveyed); MCP, A2A, ANP interoperability protocols
extraction.benchmark: REALM-Bench discussed as an example of long-horizon multi-agent evaluation; no benchmark run by the authors
extraction.key_results: PRISMA screening of 1,034 records (Scopus, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, IEEE Xplore, Jan 2020-Mar 2026) yielded 121 included studies. Contributes a framework taxonomy tracing modular chain-based execution to stateful graph-based and autonomous orchestration, a taxonomy of hierarchical, peer-to-peer, and role-based collaboration architectures, and an explicit separation of internal message-level, shared-state, and graph-based coordination from cross-system interoperability protocols (MCP for agent-to-tool, A2A for agent-to-agent, ANP for decentralized discovery, with ACP converged into A2A). Identifies error accumulation over long trajectories and cross-agent contamination as distinct multi-agent risks, and calls for intermediate verification checkpoints, confidence-aware routing, rollback, redundant agent validation, adaptive replanning, and explicit termination policies.
extraction.limitations: Narrative thematic synthesis with only qualitative methodological appraisal; no meta-analysis, effect sizes, or quantitative comparison across frameworks. The authors note that primary studies use incompatible tasks, metrics, model configurations, tool environments, and stopping conditions, which prevents direct comparison. Supplementary authoritative sources published after the March 2026 cutoff and pre-2020 foundational works were consulted but excluded from PRISMA counts. Non-English, non-peer-reviewed, and classical non-LLM multi-agent work was excluded.

records.title: LLM-Based Multi-Agent Orchestration: A Survey of Frameworks, Communication Protocols, and Emerging Patterns

evidence_notes.finding: The survey identifies an evaluation vacuum: no widely adopted benchmark targets multi-agent orchestration itself, so coordination quality, communication efficiency, delegation appropriateness, and cost are unmeasured while only task outcomes are scored. It names task duplication, contradictory outputs, and convergence failure as the three canonical coordination failure modes whose frequency rises with agent count.
evidence_notes.quote: The field evaluates what agents produce, not how well they collaborate.

extraction.framework: LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen/Microsoft Agent Framework, OpenAI Agents SDK, MetaGPT, DSPy, AgentScope, GPTSwarm, DyLAN; MCP, A2A, ANP protocols
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench and SWE-bench Verified, GAIA, WebArena, OSWorld, HumanEval, AgentBench, tau-bench (reviewed, not re-run)
extraction.baseline: human baselines on each benchmark; single-agent LLM systems as reference
extraction.key_results: Proposes a three-topology (centralized, decentralized, hierarchical) plus one adaptivity-axis taxonomy and a six-dimension coordination-quality evaluation framework. Reports large agent-human gaps: GAIA 15% for GPT-4 with plugins versus 92% human, WebArena 14.41% versus 78.24%, OSWorld 12.24% versus 72.36%, and tau-bench pass^8 reliability below 25% in retail. MetaGPT's publish-subscribe SOP design reaches 85.9% HumanEval at 124.3 tokens per line versus ChatDev's 248.9. DyLAN reports a 25.0% MMLU gain from pruning weak agents rather than adding capacity, inverting the assumption that more agents is better. Trajectory reduction cuts input tokens 40-60% within 1-2% of baseline performance. Prompt Infection shows malicious prompts self-replicating across interconnected agents, and 25 of 30 surveyed deployed agentic systems disclose no internal safety evaluation.
extraction.limitations: Explicitly a structured narrative survey rather than a systematic review, with no registered protocol, dual-reviewer screening, or GRADE evidence grading. Several headline adoption and market figures are flagged by the authors as vendor-reported or analyst projections. Most cited benchmark results used GPT-4 or GPT-4o backbones, so both absolute numbers and the relative ranking of orchestration approaches may not transfer. The authors note that self-reported efficiency claims from MetaGPT and GPTSwarm are unverified by any independent benchmark and that cross-system comparisons are rarely apples-to-apples. Literature cutoff March 2026.

records.title: A multi-agent ensemble framework for enhancing task performance using specialized LLM

evidence_notes.reason: No full text retrieved (paywalled or no open copy); explicit evidence gap. Not inferred from the abstract.

records.title: ScholForge: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Autonomous Software Engineering Research

evidence_notes.reason: No full text retrieved (paywalled or no open copy); explicit evidence gap. Not inferred from the abstract.

records.title: Multi-agent collaboration mechanisms: A survey of llms

evidence_notes.finding: The survey states the multi-agent advantage is conditional on collaboration design rather than intrinsic: well-designed collaboration channels let multi-agent systems beat single agents, but a poorly designed competitive multi-agent system can be beaten by a single agent given strong prompts.
evidence_notes.quote:
On the other hand, as studied in [ 128] MAS approach with suboptimal design for their
competitive collaboration channels can be overtaken by single-agent counterpart with
strong prompts.

extraction.framework: AutoGen, CAMEL, CrewAI, MapCoder, MACRec, Solo Performance Prompting, Auto-GPT (surveyed)
extraction.baseline: single-agent methods including chain-of-thought prompting and strongly prompted single agents
extraction.key_results: Introduces an extensible framework characterising collaboration channels by actors, type (cooperation, competition, coopetition), structure (peer-to-peer, centralized, distributed), strategy (role-based, rule-based, model-based), and coordination protocol, plus static versus dynamic orchestration architectures. Reports that sequentially chained specialist plus summarizer agents outperform single-agent chain-of-thought on college-level science questions, while noting the converse case where a suboptimally designed competitive MAS loses to a strongly prompted single agent. Distils six lessons: effective collaboration channels, collective domain knowledge, adaptive role and channel assignment, matching rule-based/role-based/model-based strategies to task type, scalability, and ethics/safety. Surveys applications across 5G/6G and Industry 5.0, question answering, and social and cultural domains.
extraction.limitations: The authors note LLMs are standalone algorithms not trained for collaboration, leaving the mechanisms by which collaboration helps unclear and agent behaviour hard to explain or predict for stakeholders. They flag safety and performance failures such as exploitation and hallucination in competitive scenarios, and rising coordination complexity, cost, and performance degradation as agent count grows. No quantitative pooling, no standardized benchmark, and no controlled single-versus-multi experiment is performed by the survey itself.

records.title: Minimizing Response Latency in LLM-Based Agent Systems: A Comprehensive Survey

evidence_notes.finding: A MetaGPT-versus-ChatDev case study shows that replacing dialogue-driven coordination with a hierarchical SOP pipeline using structured document handoffs cuts end-to-end latency by roughly 29% and simultaneously improves output executability, so coordination topology is a first-order determinant of both speed and reliability.
evidence_notes.quote:
The data in Table 11 reveals that MetaGPT completes
complex software development tasks in significantly less
time (541 s vs. 762 s on average), representing a ∼ 29%
reduction in end-to-end latency [26].

extraction.framework: MetaGPT (hierarchical SOP case study), ChatDev (chat-based baseline), DyLAN, AgentScope, TimeArena
extraction.agent_count: 5 role agents in the MetaGPT case study (Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer, QA Engineer)
extraction.benchmark: SoftwareDev benchmark (7 representative tasks, numbers sourced from the MetaGPT paper); TimeArena cited as a simulation environment
extraction.baseline: ChatDev chat-based multi-agent coordination; single-agent architectures discussed as the contrasting paradigm
extraction.key_results: Decomposes end-to-end latency into core inference, agent framework, system/infrastructure, and multi-agent coordination layers, and names five multi-agent latency sources: inter-agent communication round trips, synchronization overhead, coordination protocol delays, cascading delays in dependent tasks, and straggler heterogeneity. Case study: MetaGPT 541 s versus ChatDev 762 s (~29% lower), executability 3.75 versus 2.25 on a 1-4 scale, and human revision cost 0.83 versus 2.5 manual corrections, which the authors treat as reduced hidden latency. Reports hierarchical decomposition at 10-30 s subtask granularity achieving 50-70% critical-path latency reduction over flat structures, dynamic load balancing yielding 20-40% throughput gains, and trajectory reduction cutting input tokens 40-60% within 1-2% of original performance. Notes the rigid SOP workflow trades adaptability for speed and suits only domains with well-defined roles.
extraction.limitations: The authors state that standardized MAS latency benchmarks comparable to single-agent TTFT/TPOT do not yet exist, and that fine-grained communication and coordination overheads are not measured consistently across architectures. They explicitly note that multi-agent coordination mechanisms are rarely evaluated against single-agent baselines under controlled conditions, so the relative contribution of each optimization layer is obscured. Case-study numbers are secondary, drawn from the MetaGPT paper over only seven SoftwareDev tasks rather than independently replicated. Aggressive latency optimizations risk degrading accuracy, factual consistency, and safety, a latency-quality-safety trade-off the survey leaves unquantified, and system-level optimizations are often hardware-specific and non-portable.

records.title: Agentic AI Modernization: Transforming Institutional Infrastructure Through Orchestrated Multi-Agent LLM Framework

evidence_notes.finding: A seven-agent, on-premises AutoGen pipeline applied to 2.12M lines of COBOL, MUMPS, and PeopleSoft legacy code across three universities achieved 87% behavioural equivalence with 35% manual intervention, versus a cited single-LLM GPT-4 COBOL study where 72% of function-level translations succeeded but only 34% achieved end-to-end behavioural equivalence.
evidence_notes.quote:
An average behavioural equivalence of 87% was achieved, with the highest accuracy (91%) 
observed in the large research university deployment, confirming strong functional preservation across diverse systems 
[Table 9].

extraction.framework: AutoGen (primary, scored 8.5/10), LangGraph (secondary); custom seven-agent on-premises modernization architecture with local Llama 3/Mixtral inference
extraction.benchmark: Proprietary multi-institutional legacy corpus: 2.3M lines reduced to 1.8M analyzable lines across COBOL mainframe SIS, MUMPS registration, PeopleSoft customizations, and PL/I; 47 regulatory requirements and 3,421 test cases
extraction.baseline: Traditional manual/consultant-led modernization (65-75% manual intervention, 40-50% documentation accuracy); a cited 2024 single-LLM GPT-4 COBOL study as the monolithic comparator
extraction.key_results: 2.12M lines analyzed produced 2.04M lines of modernized Java, Python, and Go with 87% aggregate behavioural equivalence (91% / 84% / 86% by site). Manual intervention fell to 35% versus 65-75% traditional, timelines fell 65% (3,600 hours at 30 FTE to 552 hours, an 85% activity-level reduction), documentation accuracy reached 78% versus 40-50%, and 12-month cost fell from $1,105,000 to $468,000 (58%). Agent task success ranged 87.2% (code generation, 2.7 average retries) to 96.9% (compliance validation, 1.0 retries). Compliance validation reached 93.6% FERPA, 97.9% GDPR, 100% CCPA, and 95.7% institutional policy. Processing scaled near-linearly from 6.2 days at 500K lines to 17.5 days at 2.1M lines. The paper's distinctive claim is governance alignment: mapping agent tiers onto academic committees, senate subcommittees, and IT steering committees to reduce adoption resistance.
extraction.limitations: Pilot spans only three institutional partners, and the authors themselves call for 20-30 institutions before statistical generalization. No matched single-agent or single-LLM arm was run by the authors; the 65-75% manual-intervention and 40-50% documentation comparators are traditional-practice figures and the 34% end-to-end equivalence figure is drawn from a cited third-party study, so the headline contrast is not a controlled comparison. Code generation showed the highest failure and retry rates. Llama 3 context-window limits required hierarchical summarization as a workaround. All outcome metrics are self-reported from the authors' own deployment without independent verification, blinding, or variance estimates.

records.title: Multi-Agent RAG Framework for Entity Resolution: Advancing Beyond Single-LLM Approaches with Specialized Agent Coordination

evidence_notes.finding: A four-agent LangGraph RAG pipeline for entity resolution beat a single-LLM GPT-4 baseline on accuracy (93.9% vs 86.9%) while simultaneously cutting tokens ~62%, API calls >60%, and runtime 52%, attributed to selective retrieval per agent and shared state memory that avoids redundant inference.
evidence_notes.quote:
The proposed framework reduced token
usage by approximately 62% and API calls by over 60% compared to the single-LLM baseline, leading
to a 52% decrease in average runtime.

extraction.framework: LangGraph-orchestrated multi-agent RAG (Direct Matcher, Indirect Matcher, Household Matcher, Move Detector) over FAISS/Qdrant with GPT-4o-mini, Mistral, Gemini 1.5 Flash, Llama 3.2, and DeepSeek
extraction.benchmark: Synthetic S12PX administrative/census dataset segments of 200-300 records with duplicates and injected data-quality faults; precision, recall, F1, pairwise P/R, Adjusted Rand Index, runtime, and expert-rated interpretability
extraction.baseline: Single-LLM entity resolution (GPT-4); rule-based deterministic matching; FAISS-only vector similarity; hybrid no-RAG ablation; uncoordinated multi-LLM
extraction.key_results: 93.9% accuracy, 94.6% precision, 92.3% recall, 93.4% F1, versus single-LLM GPT-4 at 86.9/88.4/84.5/86.4, hybrid no-RAG at 89.2, FAISS-only at 84.6, and rule-based at 78.5. Per-agent accuracy ranged 91.3% (Move Detector) to 94.3% (Direct Matcher). Efficiency: 14,506 tokens versus 38,400, 112 API calls versus 287, and 94.5 s versus 198.4 s per 300 records. The uncoordinated multi-LLM ablation reached only 23% cost reduction versus 61% for the coordinated framework, isolating orchestration rather than agent count as the driver. Residual errors were dominated by data quality (ambiguous name variants 27%, incomplete temporal information 18%, address formatting 16%) with LLM misinterpretation and context drift accounting for only 9%, which the authors attribute to retrieval grounding suppressing hallucination.
extraction.limitations: Scalability was tested only on subsets of roughly 300 entities because of LLM context and API constraints, so production-scale behaviour on millions of records is unvalidated. Evaluation used synthetic S12PX data rather than live administrative or census records, leaving cross-source generalization untested. Agent reasoning remains sensitive to prompt wording and context-window size, prompting the authors to call for adaptive prompt optimization. Sequential inter-agent orchestration introduces latency that the authors propose to mitigate with future parallel execution. Quantitative metrics were averaged over only three runs. The retrieved full text is the Preprints.org version marked not peer reviewed.

records.title: Engineering LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems: A Taxonomy of Emerging Frameworks

evidence_notes.finding: A five-dimension taxonomy derived from 18 systematic studies and 14 frameworks finds that architectural primitives (agents, tools, memory, roles) are mature while monitoring, KPI/value-addition modelling, human feedback, continual evolution, benchmarking, and agent discovery are largely unimplemented, making the robustness of agentic software-engineering solutions hard to justify or reproduce.
evidence_notes.quote:
Governance mechanisms introduce a trade-off between
flexibility and controllability.

extraction.framework: 14 analyzed LMAS frameworks (workflow-oriented, graph-based, and tool-augmented, including LangChain/LangGraph and LlamaIndex); README summarization exemplar built on LangChain
extraction.agent_count: 4 in the README summarization exemplar (Extractor, Summarizer, Teacher, Prompt Creator)
extraction.benchmark: ROUGE-scored GitHub README 'About' summarization against curated ground-truth descriptions
extraction.baseline: Single-model README summarization, described qualitatively as struggling with heterogeneous structure and extreme length variability
extraction.key_results: Taxonomy organizes the design space into Core Architecture, Governance Rules, Agent Monitoring, Behavioral Models, and Reusability, refined from 57 initial concepts to 21 sub-concepts. Coverage analysis shows Agent, Objective, Action, and Role are supported by essentially all 18 papers and 14 frameworks, whereas Value-addition/KPI modelling appears in only 4 frameworks, Continual evolution in 1, Benchmarking in 5, Agent comparison in 6, and Discovery in 3. All surveyed frameworks support only text-based agent-environment interfaces. The exemplar pairs GPT-4o-mini for high-volume extraction and summarization with GPT-4o for reasoning-intensive teacher and prompt-creator roles, using ROUGE gates for reproducibility. The paper argues MAS should be treated as engineered software systems with explicit, comparable design decisions.
extraction.limitations: Corpus is small and narrow: 47 initial records reduced to 18 primary studies plus 14 frameworks, restricted to English systematic studies in well-ranked venues or relevant preprints from January 2023 to January 2025, searched only in Scopus, and excluding workshops, posters, non-systematic studies, and non-LLM MAS. The taxonomy is conceptual and validated only against a single illustrative README summarization case, with no controlled evaluation or inter-rater reliability reported. The authors explicitly defer security, cost management, and ethics dimensions to future work due to space limits.

records.title: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM and Single Agent LLM Efficiency for Contextual Text Generation

evidence_notes.finding: A three-agent retriever/reasoner/summarizer pipeline outscored a monolithic single-agent Gemini setup on every reference-overlap metric, but the single-agent arm answered without access to the supporting explanation documents that the multi-agent retriever consumed, so the reported gap confounds retrieval augmentation with multi-agent decomposition.
evidence_notes.quote:
As shown in the Table 1 the Multi agent system 
outperform the single agent system in every metrics.

extraction.framework: Custom single-agent versus three-agent RAG pipeline (Retriever Agent, Reasoner Agent, Summarizer Agent) on Google gemini-flash-latest
extraction.benchmark: Author-created CSV dataset of three basic science topics (photosynthesis, water cycle, respiration) with query, reference answer, and supporting explanation per row; scored with BLEU, ROUGE-1/2/L, METEOR, and BERTScore
extraction.baseline: single-agent monolithic LLM answering each query directly with no intermediate reasoning
extraction.key_results: Multi-agent beat single-agent on all six metrics: BERTScore F1 0.8978 versus 0.8117, BLEU 0.1124 versus 0.0036, METEOR 0.5867 versus 0.1749, ROUGE-1 0.5489 versus 0.0829, ROUGE-2 0.2966 versus 0.0211, ROUGE-L 0.4636 versus 0.0675. The authors conclude that LLM framework performance depends on structure and task assignment rather than model size alone, and that decomposing goals into modular subtasks reduces hallucination in complex multi-requirement tasks.
extraction.limitations: The paper reports no limitations section. Observed threats: the dataset is tiny, hand-authored, and covers only three elementary science topics; the paper states the single-agent system responded without accessing the supporting documents while the multi-agent setup retrieved, reasoned, and summarized over them, so retrieval access is confounded with architecture; no repeated runs, variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported; no token, cost, or latency measurement despite the paper's 'efficiency' framing; a single model family is used; and the reduced-hallucination claim is asserted rather than measured. The extracted text also contains a garbled encoded column alongside a readable one.

records.title: Training-Free Agentic AI: Probabilistic Control and Coordination in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

evidence_notes.finding: Because the split-knowledge tasks are constructed so no single agent can solve them, the study deliberately omits any single-agent baseline and instead isolates routing: belief-guided Thompson-sampling delegation matched random delegation on success (96.65% vs 96.46%) while using 0.72x tokens, 0.83x agent calls, and 0.81x time-to-success.
evidence_notes.quote:
Since split-knowledge tasks are unsolvable by any single
agent, single-agent baselines are excluded by task design.

extraction.framework: REDEREF: training-free controller with Thompson-sampling belief-guided delegation, calibrated LLM/programmatic judge, evidence-based selection, and memory-aware priors
extraction.agent_count: 16 (6 specialist RAG agents plus 10 generalist conversational agents)
extraction.benchmark: Author-constructed split-knowledge benchmark synthesized in three stages so each task requires non-redundant contributions from 4-6 agents; Azure OpenAI endpoints with fixed seeds

extraction.agent_count: 6 (4 specialists + Moderator + Judge)
extraction.benchmark: Mendeley Phishing Websites dataset and TR-OP dataset, 500 phishing plus 500 legitimate samples each; TPR, TNR, FPR, FNR, precision, recall, accuracy, F1, and inference time

records.title: Risk analysis techniques for governed LLM-based multi-agent systems

evidence_notes.finding: The report argues multi-agent deployment transforms rather than merely adds to the risk landscape, naming six failure modes (cascading reliability failures, inter-agent communication failures, monoculture collapse, conformity bias, deficient theory of mind, mixed-motive dynamics), and prescribes explicit single-agent baselining to test whether coordination actually improves performance at all.
evidence_notes.quote:
Compare multi-agent outcomes against individual agents
working on decomposable portions of the task to determine if coordination actually
improves performance.

extraction.baseline: Recommends four reference baselines: single-agent performance on decomposable task portions, human team benchmarks, theoretical optima, and historical performance at initial deployment
extraction.key_results: Defines four canonical settings (single-agent equivalent, centralized orchestrator with specialised delegates, collaborative swarm, distributed autonomous task force) and maps six failure modes onto them. Argues that a collection of safe agents does not guarantee a safe collection of agents, and that every multi-agent system inherits single-agent failure modes plus additional cascading and emergent layers, making single-agent analysis an essential baseline. Centres risk analysis on validity - construct, external, content, and consequential - pursued through progressively increasing convergent evidence across simulations, observational data analysis, benchmarking against baselines, red teaming, and capability benchmarking, with staged testing that gradually increases exposure. Notes that in a centralized orchestrator the orchestrator's cognitive limits become system-wide bottlenecks because delegates lack visibility of the full task. Red-teaming recipes include malformed instructions, contradictory goals, information asymmetries, and inserting a malfunctioning or adversarial agent to test cascade resilience. Also flags LLM-judge calibration against human-annotated samples and recalibration whenever task content, network topology, or base models change.
extraction.limitations: A practitioner guidance report rather than an empirical study: it contributes no experiments, datasets, measured effect sizes, or validated instruments, and the authors position the techniques as adaptable tools rather than a prescriptive framework. Scope is restricted to governed environments where a single organisation controls the configuration and deployment of all agents, so open, cross-organisational, or adversarial multi-agent ecosystems are excluded. The authors acknowledge fundamental limits in the scientific understanding of LLM behaviour, so practitioners can only progressively increase validity rather than establish it. Translation from risk analysis to risk evaluation and treatment is left highly contextual and organisation-specific. Coverage of catastrophic risk, security, privacy, and human-AI interaction is discussed only briefly.

evidence_notes.finding: The review separates tool-augmented single "AI Agents" from multi-agent "Agentic AI" and argues each paradigm has its own failure profile: single agents suffer hallucination, shallow planning and prompt brittleness, while multi-agent systems add inter-agent misalignment, error cascades, emergent unpredictability and debugging opacity. extraction.baseline: AI Agents (single, tool-augmented LLM agents) contrasted conceptually with Agentic AI multi-agent systems
extraction.key_results: Proposes a conceptual taxonomy separating AI Agents (modular, task-specific, tool-calling LLM agents) from Agentic AI (multi-agent collaboration, dynamic task decomposition, persistent memory, coordinated autonomy). Catalogues paradigm-specific challenges: for single agents hallucination, shallow reasoning, limited planning depth and prompt brittleness; for multi-agent systems inter-agent distributional shift, error cascades from one hallucinating agent through downstream agents, communication/coordination bottlenecks from loosely defined natural-language protocols, resource contention and race conditions, unpredictable emergent behaviour including infinite planning loops and action deadlocks, and non-compositionality where extra agents add noise and coordination overhead rather than capability. records.title: A Comparative Study Towards Designing a Hybrid Architecture of Microservices and LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

evidence_notes.finding: A structured architectural comparison of microservice systems against LLM-based multi-agent systems, which grounds LLM-MAS failure in design and coordination rather than model quality, and proposes microservice engineering practices (layered separation of concerns, fallback agents, CI/CD test suites, RBAC) as transferable mitigations.
evidence_notes.quote: The MAST taxonomy reveals that failures in LLM-MAS are primarily due to systematic design and coordination issues, rather than simply the limitation of individual LLMs or prompts.

extraction.baseline: microservice systems (deterministic, contract-based execution) compared against LLM-based multi-agent systems
extraction.key_results: Contrasts the two paradigms across eight architectural dimensions (function encapsulation, orchestration, API design, auto-correction, data communication, environment awareness, DevOps vs AgentOps, quality attributes). Key mismatches: microservice boundaries are human-defined and discrete while agent encapsulation is fluid and roles overlap; microservice failover relies on stateless replication and health checks whereas stateful agents have no well-defined failover and each agent can be a single point of failure; microservice scaling is resource-driven while agent scaling is task-driven; microservice consistency is data consistency while LLM-MAS consistency is belief and objective alignment, motivating a weaker LCAP alternative to CAP. Evaluation metrics must shift from latency/throughput SLIs to goal convergence, hallucination rate, belief-drift rate and dialogue turns to alignment. Four open research questions are defined covering microservice semantic comprehension, agent racing and reasoning inconsistency over shared services, hybrid observability and root-cause analysis, and hybrid benchmarking.
extraction.limitations: Purely analytical comparative study with no implementation, benchmark or empirical measurement; the proposed hybrid architecture and the four research questions are stated as future work, and the transferable best practices are argued rather than validated.

extraction.framework: SALLMA (Software Architecture for LLM-Based Multi-Agent systems)
extraction.baseline: single-agent LLM systems (argued conceptually; no controlled comparison run)
extraction.key_results: Two-layer reference architecture applying Fowler's Reflection pattern: an Operational Layer (Intent Management Agent, Workflow Management Agent, Routing Manager, Deployment Manager, Cognitive Workflow Manager) and a Knowledge Layer (workflow metamodel catalog, LLM configuration catalog, deployment metamodel catalog). evidence_notes.finding: A literature review concluding that multi-agent role specialization buys scalability and parallelism over single agents but introduces coordination overhead and new failure modes, and that benchmark success rates systematically overstate real-world engineering value.

records.title: Trust-Aware Multi-Agent Traceability: Confidence-Calibrated Knowledge Graphs for Consistent Software Artifact Management

evidence_notes.finding: In a sequential multi-agent artifact pipeline, upstream low-confidence decisions propagate downstream, so the paper turns calibrated confidence into a first-class coordination signal: threshold gating, divergence detection between derivation-time and validation-time confidence, and conflict materialization as graph nodes.
evidence_notes.quote: In this pipeline, errors and low-confidence decisions made by upstream agents propagate to downstream stages: poorly seeded traceability links lead to misaligned components, which in turn produce inadequate tests.

extraction.framework: trust-aware multi-agent traceability framework over a Neo4j confidence-calibrated knowledge graph
extraction.agent_count: 5 (Requirement, Architect, Traceability, Test, Analysis agents)
extraction.benchmark: custom automotive case study of 535 artifacts across six subsystems (AEB, LKA, BMS, IVI, V2X, DMS): 83 system requirements, 128 software requirements, 124 components, 200 test specifications with human-validated ground-truth traceability matrices
extraction.baseline: TF-IDF + cosine lexical matching, embedding-only retrieval, unfiltered LLM-only evaluation; plus ablations with and without consistency controls
extraction.key_results: The two-stage pipeline (semantic retrieval then LLM multi-criteria analysis) reached F1 0.769 versus 0.669 for LLM-only and 0.349 for TF-IDF, a 13% F1 gain attributed to pre-filtering 200+ candidate pairs down to k~10 before LLM reasoning. Relationship-specific results: REF_BY precision 1.000 and F1 0.842, IMP_BY F1 0.833, VER_BY F1 0.706 (weakest, due to behavioural versus functional vocabulary mismatch). A 120-configuration ablation found (tau=0.5, epsilon=0.4) uniquely detected all 10 ground-truth conflicts with zero false positives across all configurations, and showed dataset-dependent parameter dominance so no single-parameter tuning is globally optimal. The full consistency stack held graph inflation to 1.46 versus 3.94 without controls while exposing a 15.42% conflict rate and reducing conflict-aware path completeness to 33.64%. Link creation threshold 0.7 was optimal (precision 0.782, recall 0.818, F1 0.796, 23 links per dataset for manual review).
extraction.limitations: Evaluation limited to automotive systems (535 artifacts, 6 subsystems) in safety-critical regulatory contexts; generalisation to larger codebases is untested; the divergence threshold delta is set by domain expert judgement rather than empirically tuned; the bootstrap problem of confidence calibration in domains lacking ground truth remains open; conflict resolution is not automated.

records.title: Reducing Cost of LLM Agents with Trajectory Reduction

evidence_notes.finding: Coding-agent trajectories accumulate useless, redundant and expired content that dominates cost; removing it at inference time via a separate reflection module cuts input tokens 39.9-59.7% and total cost 21.1-35.9% while holding resolve rate within -1.0% to +2.0%, contradicting the assumed token-efficiency versus performance trade-off.
evidence_notes.quote: After we further consider the computational overhead of the reflection module itself ($+), the final cost reduction becomes 21.1%–35.9%.

extraction.framework: AgentDiet, implemented on the Trae Agent
extraction.agent_count: 1 coding agent plus 1 auxiliary LLM reflection module
extraction.benchmark: SWE-bench Verified and Multi-SWE-bench Flash (seven programming languages)
extraction.baseline: the Original unmodified agent with no trajectory reduction, on Claude 4 Sonnet and Gemini 2.5 Pro
extraction.key_results: The reflection module removes 69.2-77.4% of the content it processes, reducing accumulated input tokens by 39.9-59.7%, raw compute cost by 28.6-44.1%, and cost including reflection overhead by 21.1-35.9% (average US$ per instance falling from 0.535/0.385/1.277/0.701 to 0.422/0.285/0.933/0.449). Resolve rate is comparable (-1.0% to +2.0%) and step counts do not increase. A pilot analysis found the average SWE-bench Verified trajectory holds 48.4K tokens over 40 steps, of which 30.4K are tool messages, with accumulated per-issue token usage reaching 1.0M. An unexpected robustness benefit: with Gemini 2.5 Pro on Multi-SWE-bench Flash, instances hitting the 100-step limit fell from 66 to 26 and average steps from 57.20 to 43.90, because long contexts had been causing repeated invalid tool calls. Results generalise across two benchmarks, two LLMs and seven languages.
extraction.limitations: AgentDiet was implemented for only one agent system (Trae Agent) because experiments already cost roughly US$2000, so cross-agent generalisation is assumed from agent homogeneity rather than measured. Proprietary LLMs raise a data-leakage threat, mitigated by adding the third-party Multi-SWE-bench Flash. Test-based validation admits plausible-but-incorrect patches, an overfitting threat shared with the baseline. Latency was not quantitatively compared because commercial API latency is unstable, and the off-the-shelf reflection LLM still incurs 5-10% cost overhead.

records.title: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems

evidence_notes.finding: A controlled 180-configuration comparison of single-agent versus four multi-agent topologies across four agentic benchmarks derives quantitative scaling principles: a tool-coordination trade-off, a capability saturation point around 45% single-agent accuracy beyond which coordination gives negative returns, and topology-dependent error amplification of 17.2x (independent) versus 4.4x (centralized).
evidence_notes.quote: Yet for sequential reasoning tasks, every multi-agent variant we tested degraded performance by 39–70%.

extraction.agent_count: typically small teams, with preliminary scaling explored up to nine agents
extraction.benchmark: FinanceAgent, BrowseComp-Plus, PlanCraft and Workbench (financial reasoning, web navigation, game planning, workflow execution)
extraction.baseline: Single-Agent System (SAS) compared against four multi-agent architectures (Independent, Centralized, Decentralized, Hybrid) with standardized tools, prompt structures and token budgets
extraction.key_results: 180 configurations across three LLM families. A mixed-effects model over coordination metrics (efficiency, error amplification, message density, redundancy) achieves cross-validated R^2=0.524 and predicts the optimal architecture for 87% of held-out configurations; out-of-sample validation on GPT-5.2, Gemini-3.0 Pro and Flash gives MAE=0.077 and confirms three of five principles generalise. Three dominant effects: (1) tool-coordination trade-off (beta=-0.267, p<0.001) where tool-heavy tasks suffer disproportionately from coordination overhead because the per-agent token budget is fragmented; (2) capability saturation (beta=-0.404, p<0.001) where coordination yields diminishing or negative returns once single-agent baselines exceed roughly 45%; (3) topology-dependent error amplification, 17.2x for independent agents (95% CI 14.3-20.1) versus 4.4x under centralized validation bottlenecks. Benefits are task-contingent: centralized coordination improves parallelizable financial reasoning by 80.8%, decentralized coordination gains +9.2% on dynamic web navigation versus +0.2% centralized, while every multi-agent variant degraded sequential planning by 39-70%. Multi-agent systems impose intrinsic information fragmentation because global context must be compressed into inter-agent messages.
extraction.limitations: Only canonical coordination structures were compared, with agent-count scaling explored preliminarily to nine; communication overhead grows superlinearly and coordination efficiency degrades beyond moderate team sizes, so emergent behaviour in larger collectives is untested. Heterogeneity experiments mixed models only within the same family with identical base architectures. Prompts were held identical across conditions rather than optimised per model. The four benchmarks may not span the full range of agentic task characteristics, and specialized coordination protocols for tool-intensive tasks remain undeveloped.

records.title: A Multi-Agent LLM Environment for Software Design and Refactoring: A Conceptual Framework

evidence_notes.finding: A conceptual framework arguing that single-agent refactoring optimises one quality attribute at the expense of others, and that domain-specialized agents (performance, security, maintainability, UI/UX) negotiating through consensus or auction protocols can reconcile conflicting objectives; the evaluation is proposed rather than executed.
evidence_notes.quote: Preliminary experimental design is outlined to demonstrate how multi-agent interactions may resolve conflicting design goals more effectively than a single-agent approach.

extraction.framework: Multi-Agent LLM Environment for software design and refactoring (unnamed conceptual framework)
extraction.agent_count: 4 specialized agents (Performance, Security, Maintainability, UI/UX) plus a communication/coordination layer
extraction.baseline: proposed but not executed: a single general-purpose LLM (GPT-4) providing refactoring suggestions, and traditional static analysers (SonarQube, ESLint)
extraction.key_results: Formalises agent interaction with a state space, per-agent action and utility functions, a coordination protocol and an explicit termination condition (max rounds, improvement below epsilon, or all agents reporting no further proposals). Communication complexity is O(R x n x m) messages for both consensus and auction protocols, with auction reducing pairwise overhead. A motivating microservices example claims a single agent's caching and parallelisation optimisation would cut CPU from 95% to 40% while introducing unbounded cache growth, unsanitised cache keys, missing rate limiting and missing access controls, whereas a three-agent collaboration achieves 65% CPU reduction while preserving security. Proposed evaluation metrics span maintainability, performance, security scanning, UX heuristics and developer satisfaction.
extraction.limitations: The work is explicitly conceptual with no implementation or empirical validation; the authors flag hallucination and amplified error propagation when agents build on erroneous proposals, security gaps against zero-day and domain-specific threats, accountability and traceability questions when automated refactoring introduces bugs, and resource-intensive coordination overhead requiring incremental scoping, cached analyses and threshold-based agent activation.

records.title: An LLM-based multi-agent framework for agile effort estimation

evidence_notes.finding: A role-specialized LLM agent framework for planning-poker effort estimation beats deep-learning state of the art on three of four projects after project-specific fine-tuning, but the accuracy comparison deliberately isolates a single agent, so the multi-agent discussion mechanism is evaluated only through a 12-participant human study.
evidence_notes.quote: When comparing against the current state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches, SEEAgentfine-tuned outperforms in three out of four projects.

extraction.framework: SEEAgent (Software Effort Estimation Agent)
extraction.agent_count: 1 agent in the accuracy benchmark; 2 role-specialized agents (front-end and back-end developer personas) alongside 3 human developers and a human product owner in the human study
extraction.benchmark: Fine-SE dataset of four open-source Jira projects (Mesos, Data Management, Talend Data Quality, Usergrid; 4,907 stories); eShope project with 33 user stories for the human study
extraction.baseline: Deep-SE, GPT2SP and Fine-SE; plus base Llama-3.1-8B-instruct versus its fine-tuned variant
extraction.key_results: Fine-tuning transformed accuracy: DM MAE 17.053 to 4.251, ME MAE 7.398 to 1.217 (83.55% improvement), US MAE 11.300 to 0.350 with PRED(50) rising from 0.05 to 1.000. Against state of the art, the fine-tuned agent won on DM (MMRE 1.491 vs 1.739), ME (MAE 1.217, MMRE 0.414, PRED(50) 0.747, best on all metrics) and US (MAE 0.350, MMRE 0.085, PRED(50) 1.000), but lost to Deep-SE and Fine-SE on TD (MAE 5.133), attributed to only 72 fine-tuning samples and high story-point variance. Wilcoxon tests with Vargha-Delaney effect sizes show significance on US (p<0.001, 0.90-0.95), moderate effects on DM and ME (0.53-0.67), and no significant improvement on TD. The 12-participant human study reported overwhelmingly positive experience, with participants agreeing the agents help reach consensus, bridge knowledge gaps and promote communication.
extraction.limitations: The authors identify the choice of foundational LLM as an internal validity threat since different models may reason differently. The accuracy comparison deliberately evaluates SEEAgent in a standalone single-agent configuration to match prior work, so multi-agent communication and interactive refinement are not measured quantitatively. The human study has only 12 participants on a small simplified e-commerce project with discussion capped at two rounds, and the paper notes comprehensive ablation studies remain future work.

records.title: "ENERGY STAR" LLM-Enabled Software Engineering Tools

evidence_notes.finding: Measuring real-time energy and inference time for RAG-augmented code generation across four LLMs (125M-7B), the effect of retrieval augmentation on energy is model-dependent rather than size-dependent: two models got cheaper, two got more expensive.
evidence_notes.quote: The findings showed reductions in energy consumption when using RAG for GPT-2 and CodeLlama.

extraction.framework: RAG plus prompt-engineering framework with CodeCarbon energy monitoring (unnamed)
extraction.benchmark: CodeXGLUE CONCODE text-to-code subset (Java) and a Kaggle natural-language-to-Python code dataset
extraction.baseline: the same LLMs prompted without retrieval augmentation
extraction.key_results: Across GPT-2 (125M), CodeLlama (7B), Qwen 2.5 (7B) and DeepSeek Coder: RAG reduced energy for GPT-2 and CodeLlama but increased it for DeepSeek Coder and Qwen. Only CodeLlama improved inference time (25% faster with RAG) while also reducing energy and substantially improving code quality. DeepSeek Coder and Qwen consumed roughly 3x more energy than GPT-2 overall. No relationship was found between model size and RAG-based energy benefit. RAG let GPT-2 reach a code quality score of 0.6 on the Kaggle dataset, matching DeepSeek Coder while using about 3.5x less energy.
extraction.limitations: Two-page extended abstract reporting a proof of concept on a small, pragmatically chosen model set. CO2 estimates are deliberately not relied upon because the energy source is unknown. Code quality is assessed with an ad hoc score; the authors plan to add established metrics such as CodeBLEU plus static and dynamic analysis, and to move to more powerful and cloud servers where provider infrastructure could confound measurements.

records.title: Safe and Scalable Collaboration in Multiagent LLM Systems: A Comprehensive Review

evidence_notes.finding: A four-pillar review (coordination, communication, safety, alignment) that synthesises documented multi-agent deployment failures into a cross-system taxonomy, including a coordination-overhead threshold at which added modularity becomes net-negative, semantic drift and herding in long-running systems, and collective harms absent from any individual agent.
evidence_notes.quote: In frameworks of this kind, modularity can become counterproductive beyond a critical threshold.

extraction.framework: the trust stack (proposed five-layer framework: epistemic reliability, behavioral alignment, role awareness, social accountability, institutional governance)
extraction.baseline: prior single-agent alignment surveys and traditional AI safety frameworks, contrasted with multiagent-specific analysis
extraction.key_results: Organises multiagent LLM research around coordination strategies, communication frameworks, safety challenges and trust/alignment, then models their interdependencies (for example semantic drift cascading into hallucination propagation, and task-decomposition depth bounding the blast radius of misalignment). The cross-system failure taxonomy covers long-horizon diagnostic convergence and herding with semantic drift in medical simulation, a coordination-overhead threshold where net productivity is lost once inter-agent communication time exceeds twice execution time (with an illustrative optimal team size of 3-10 agents and roughly 12 files per module), and collective toxicity amplification in decentralized graph-structured collectives where group outputs contain unsafe content absent from any individual agent. Multiagent-specific vulnerabilities analysed include prompt injection propagation, perceptual adversarial cascades, reward misalignment, operational overreach and adversarial amplification through consensus. The trust stack is presented with runtime-computable metrics, formal cross-layer dependency chains and ten open research problems.
extraction.limitations: The authors state explicitly that the numerical values in the empirical failure analysis are illustrative, chosen to make qualitative failure patterns concrete, rather than measurements reported by the cited systems; the consolidated regularities and design principles are the authors' own cross-system synthesis. The trust stack itself is proposed rather than empirically validated in deployment.

records.title: Developing and Evaluating an LLM-based Agent for ExplorViz Using CopilotKit

evidence_notes.finding: A controlled usability study of an LLM assistant embedded in a software visualization tool found a sharp reliability split: deterministic tool-grounded actions were rated near-perfect, while open-ended agent-driven editing scored only 3.00/5 for expectation match with high variance, motivating guardrails such as staged previews, explicit edit scoping and undo support.
evidence_notes.quote: Editing was rated lower and showed higher variance across participants.

extraction.framework: LLM assistant embedded in ExplorViz via CopilotKit, backed by Claude Sonnet 4.5
extraction.baseline: manual ExplorViz UI interaction without the assistant, as a within-subject baseline for tasks 2-5 (task 6 had no manual baseline)
extraction.key_results: With 11 participants on a distributed PetClinic landscape: service summaries rated 4.64/5 and explanations 4.55/5 for perceived correctness; agent-triggered bulk highlighting scored 5.00/5 correctness (SD 0.00, all participants reporting no mistakes) and 4.82/5 ease-of-use versus manual; theme generation 4.27/5 expectation match and 4.82/5 ease-of-use; chat UI ease-of-use 5.00/5 and overall experience 4.36/5. Agent-driven editing was the weak point: 3.00/5 expectation match (SD 1.41, 4/11 positive), 3.27/5 perceived correctness (SD 1.49) and 3.73/5 explanation quality, with participants describing the repeated confirmation step as annoying. Resource accounting: 11,401,606 input and 135,431 output tokens for a total API cost of $36.24 with no prompt caching.
extraction.limitations: Fixed task ordering (manual first, agent second) can inflate perceived agent performance through learning effects. Most outcomes are self-reported perceptions, and perceived correctness does not imply factual correctness, particularly for summarisation. Small sample (N=11) dominated by programmers already familiar with LLM tools, a single example system, and a single model choice. The in-person controlled lab setup with a local feature branch may underestimate performance variability and integration challenges in production deployments.

records.title: LLM-assisted development of Rust for high-performance bioinformatics software: practices, workflows, and boundaries

evidence_notes.finding: Across three real Rust migration projects the authors observed three recurring agentic-coding failure modes — layer misidentification, semantic drift in script migration, and goal substitution in agentic loops — all sharing the structure that the agent optimises observable surface features while the true defect sits one abstraction level below. The countermeasure is process rather than model: every agentic iteration must introduce at least one fresh test constraint or input fixture, otherwise the loop overfits to the static test suite.
evidence_notes.quote: This is goal substitution, in which the declared goal ("make the program correct") is silently replaced by the operationalized subgoal ("make this test pass on this input").

extraction.framework: hickit_rs developed under a tiered SDD + TDD + multimodel-exploration workflow with an agentic IDE (Claude Code); replicated on sradb_rs and fastqc-rs
extraction.agent_count: 1 (single agentic coding assistant; multi-agent closed-loop systems only cited as related work)
extraction.benchmark: custom Hi-C throughput benchmark on the SRR1658573 dataset (100M and 1B read pairs)
extraction.baseline: legacy Bash/AWK reference pipeline (Juicer calculate_map_resolution.sh) as correctness oracle and performance baseline
extraction.key_results: hickit_rs reaches an 8.3-10x speedup and 86-88% peak-memory reduction versus the Bash/AWK pipeline. Three recurring AI failure modes are documented with root causes and countermeasures; goal substitution was diagnosed by inspecting the agent's visible reasoning chain, where phrases such as 'to satisfy this test' act as early warning signals. The paper cites evidence that closed-loop multi-agent systems separating test generation, execution, failure analysis and patch review achieve higher coverage and lower invalid-test rates than single-agent baselines, and argues the central challenge has shifted from prompt engineering to process engineering.
extraction.limitations: Perspective article grounded in the authors' own three projects with no controlled experiment, no statistics and no inter-rater validation. Failure modes are argued to be amplified by bioinformatics-specific format semantics (multimember gzip, BGZF, AWK boundary conventions) absent from generic benchmarks, so generality is asserted rather than demonstrated. Cross-platform determinism still depends on target configuration and libc/musl choices; static linking mitigates but does not eliminate this. The authors explicitly do not advocate rewriting all tools in Rust.

records.title: A Research Roadmap for Augmenting Software Engineering Processes and Software Products with Generative AI

evidence_notes.finding: The roadmap classifies GenAI augmentation into four forms (Copilot, GenAIware, Teammate, Robot) and finds that the agentic 'GenAI Teammate' form enhances speed, prototyping and time-to-market but reverses Git versioning semantics, environmental sustainability, accountability and code ownership, and code comprehension. Inter-agent communication overhead is identified as a direct driver of energy cost, and multi-agent systems are flagged as capable of pursuing conflicting goals that must be planned for explicitly.
evidence_notes.quote: Multi-agent systems may also pursue conflicting goals that should be taken into account when planning the overall system behavior.

extraction.key_results: Design-science roadmap over three cycles combining the FSE 2025 'Software Engineering 2030' workshop, rapid literature reviews and external feedback, using McLuhan tetrads. For the agentic Teammate form it reports that most architectures do not parallelize code generation but streamline a pipeline of specialized agents, which reverses the purpose of Git versioning; that accountability remains unresolved for fully autonomous systems, mitigated only by RACI-style rules requiring a human 'Accountable' actor whenever an LLM-based multi-agent system is 'Responsible'; and that communication overhead between LLM instances carries significant energy and sustainability cost. 2030 predictions include at least five multi-agent orchestration platforms with standardized agent-to-agent protocols, the '10x developer' becoming a '10x orchestrator', and 60% of maintenance effort going to AI-generated code.
extraction.limitations: Evidence base is rapid rather than full systematic literature reviews, so coverage is incomplete. Tetrad construction and the roadmap synthesis are author-judgement driven, mitigated only by cross-validation among independent author teams and peers. The 2030 predictions are extrapolations, not measured trends. The authors devote a dedicated section to validity risks in a fast-moving field.

records.title: Developing Multi-Agent LLM Applications Through Continuous Human-LLM Co-Programming

evidence_notes.finding: COPMA's refactoring patterns treat autonomy as a tunable dial: an autonomous group-manager agent planning workflows produces task misassignment and missing context, so the authors deliberately trade flexibility for predictability by fixing execution order, adding a moderator agent, or replacing the manager with code that orchestrates agents programmatically. Shifting implementations from the 'LLM world' to the 'code world' is presented as the main lever for controlling unpredictability and cost.
evidence_notes.quote: A group manager agent can autonomously plan and coordinate workflows among agents, but this can lead to task misassignment or missing context.

extraction.framework: COPMA (feature-block models plus co-programming patterns), built on AutoGen 0.2.35 with GPT-4o
extraction.agent_count: 6 agents plus 21 code blocks
extraction.baseline: the same developer's estimate of traditional manual development effort (40+ hours)
extraction.key_results: A medical-literature snowballing application was decomposed into 38 features across four layers implemented as 6 agents and 21 Python code blocks with 27 prompts and 552 lines of code (~350 LLM-generated), over 80 iterations in 18 effective hours across 8 days versus an estimated 40+ hours traditionally. records.title: When Code Becomes Abundant: Redefining Software Engineering Around Orchestration and Verification

evidence_notes.finding: The paper argues the SDLC is being compressed between cheap AI code generation and hardening physical/regulatory constraints, collapsing construction and routine maintenance into two remaining poles of human responsibility: orchestration (intent articulation and architectural control) and verification. Its central named risk is 'accountability collapse' — the erosion of the link between human decisions and system behaviour when automated synthesis rather than manual design determines software structure — with architecture repositioned as a governance control surface that preserves traceability.
evidence_notes.quote: These boundaries are essential for preventing accountability collapse: they preserve traceability between intent, generation, and observed behavior, and define where responsibility can be meaningfully located.

extraction.key_results: Proposes a reorganization table in which requirements become continuous intent modeling, architecture becomes a control surface enabling traceability, testing becomes executable specification and the primary trust mechanism, maintenance becomes continuous verification across regenerations, and security becomes both a generation constraint and adversarial validation. Argues regeneration makes maintenance more dangerous, not simpler, because systems become reproducible yet poorly understood and evolution becomes opaque even when snapshots are auditable. Calls for intent logs alongside code repositories, architectural review gates before and after synthesis, and dedicated 'regeneration auditors', plus research on formal intent specification, misalignment detection, verification that scales to continuously regenerated systems, and maintainability metrics for regeneration.
extraction.limitations: Position paper with no empirical study, dataset or evaluation. The central motivating case (a $50 million loss from weekly-regenerated risk modules) is a hypothetical illustration rather than an observed incident. Claims about accountability collapse and SDLC compression are argued from cited productivity figures and hardware-scaling trends rather than measured. Proposed practices such as regeneration auditors are untested.

records.title: ATeam: Governance-Aware LLM-Assisted Software Sustaining Engineering for Enterprise Systems

evidence_notes.finding: In a controlled comparison on 24 IEEE 14764 maintenance tasks over a seven-service microservice testbed, governed template-driven execution beat both an AutoGPT-style structured-reasoning agent and unconstrained prompting with huge effect sizes, while the difference between the agentic baseline and plain prompting was statistically negligible. This is direct evidence that agentic orchestration by itself does not improve sustaining-engineering outcomes; decomposition, dependency analysis and approval gates do.
evidence_notes.quote: The evidence suggests that governance, rather than agentic execution alone, is the primary determinant of reliable enterprise software sustaining engineering.

extraction.framework: ATeam (governance-aware multi-phase pipeline: analysis, planning, execution, validation, finalization, driven by ChangeType YAML templates)
extraction.benchmark: 24 IEEE 14764-aligned sustaining-engineering templates executed against a 7-service microservice system; 216 task executions (3 models x 3 runs x 24 tasks), scored by rule-based checks plus a GPT-5-Codex rubric judge
extraction.baseline: AutoGPT-style structured-reasoning agent baseline and an unconstrained prompting baseline, both executing identical intents without ChangeType decomposition, dependency analysis or governance gates
extraction.key_results: At 20B, ATeam scored 82.58 weighted versus 63.19 for structured reasoning and 60.39 unconstrained; at 2B the gap was widest (69.10 vs 23.06 vs 21.24). Welch's t-tests give ATeam vs structured reasoning p=6.5e-4 (Cohen's d=2.23) and ATeam vs unconstrained p=2.7e-4 (d=2.49), while structured reasoning vs unconstrained is not significant (p=0.69, d=0.19). No monotonic relationship holds between parameter count and pass rate or aggregate score: Granite 2B is competitive with and sometimes more stable than gpt-oss-20b, supporting on-premises small-model deployment in regulated industries. Perfective and preventive categories score lower than adaptive and corrective. Pass-rate variance across replications exceeds rubric and weighted-score variance even at fixed model size. Overall governance yields 1.3-3.3x better reliability than the baselines.
extraction.limitations: Governance approval gates ran in auto-approval mode to isolate framework behaviour, so human-in-the-loop performance is speculated rather than measured. Scoring relies on an LLM judge (GPT-5-Codex) with acknowledged potential systematic bias, validated only against expert review on n=20 (95% agreement). The testbed is a purpose-built microservice system rather than a real enterprise brownfield codebase. Only three model sizes and three runs each. The authors attribute some failures to template quality rather than model capability.

records.title: Human-AI experience in integrated development environments: a systematic literature review

evidence_notes.finding: A PRISMA systematic review of 90 in-IDE human-AI experience studies finds that productivity gains from AI coding assistance are consistently accompanied by a verification tax: developers spend more time checking output, and reliance miscalibrates in both directions (novices over-rely and under-verify, professionals under-rely and reject correct output lacking a rationale). Research is heavily concentrated on GitHub Copilot and the implementation stage, leaving requirements, testing and deployment largely unstudied.
evidence_notes.quote: Impact findings show that AI-assisted coding enhances developer productivity but also introduces challenges, such as verification overhead and over-reliance.

extraction.key_results: 257 studies screened, 90 reviewed, organized into Impact (74/90), Design (28/90) and Quality (19/90). Impact studies report productivity improvements, especially for experienced users, alongside verification overhead and over-reliance. Trust rises with high-quality context-relevant suggestions and falls with inconsistency and unnecessary complexity; trust drops for high-stakes and production work and for complex open-ended tasks, and developers accept completions less readily in test files than production files. Design studies identify autocompletion and conversational assistance as complementary rather than competing paradigms and converge on three principles: context awareness, explainability/transparency, and user control/adaptability. Quality studies document correctness, maintainability and security risks and call for stronger validation and diagnostic support. The stated future agenda prioritizes productivity factors (43 mentions), design of AI assistance (29) and audits of AI-generated code (28), with larger and longer evaluations.
extraction.limitations: Self-reported threats include sampling bias toward professional contexts from a recall-oriented query, temporal bias from the 2022-2024 window, source-reliability risk from including non-peer-reviewed arXiv papers, and interpretation bias in categorizing 90 studies. The authors also note that the underlying primary studies favour short-term evaluations with underpowered samples and limited contextual variation, and that industrial research timelines discourage statistically rigorous designs. The review covers in-IDE assistants rather than autonomous or multi-agent systems.
